articles.title: Iran widens Gulf attacks by targeting a U.S. air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain
articles.summary: CAIRO — Iran widened its attacks on its Gulf neighbors on Wednesday, targeting a U.S. air base in Kuwait and launching several attacks on Bahrain in what appeared to be retaliation for American strikes the day before.
articles.body: CAIRO — Iran widened its attacks on its Gulf neighbors on Wednesday, targeting a U.S. air base in Kuwait and launching several attacks on Bahrain in what appeared to be retaliation for American strikes the day before. After about two months without such attacks, Iran has repeatedly targeted U.S. facilities in Bahrain in recent days. The small Persian Gulf island kingdom hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet. The early morning attacks in the nearly nine-month-old war came after a U.S. fighter jet struck a Revolutionary Guard missile launch site Tuesday on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. strike was in retaliation for an Iranian attack on an American radar installation in Bahrain earlier Tuesday. Iran said that its recent attacks — including those on other U.S. facilities in Bahrain on Sunday and Friday — were in response to U.S. drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers. The tit-for-tat attacks come as the commander of the U.S. military’s Central Command, Adm. Brad Cooper, met Wednesday in Tel Aviv with Israel’s military chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, and the director of Israel’s intelligence agency Mossad, Roman Gofman. They also complicate negotiations for a diplomatic solution and raise the risk of resumption of all-out conflict as a conflict in Yemen between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi-led coalition could drag on for months. The U.S. military didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest attacks. Blockade puts pressure on Tehran With its economy suffering under a U.S. naval blockade and American military escorts helping restore the passage of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, experts say that the recent attacks suggest Tehran may be growing weary of the status quo. “Even if neither side intends to enter a broader confrontation, the accumulation of military incidents across multiple fronts increases the risk of miscalculation and escalation beyond what either side originally intended,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X following the initial reports of the attack on Kuwait. U.S. President Donald Trump has sent mixed messages on his next steps, saying new strikes are highly unlikely, but also sending a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East. Though U.S. military protection has helped restore oil shipments from the Gulf, Iran has continued to attack tankers as they attempt to transit the Strait of Hormuz. United Arab Emirates state-owned oil company ADNOC said Wednesday that one of its tanker crew members was missing after an attack in the strait on Tuesday, while 11 others were injured and were receiving medical care. Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, described an “increasingly clear” pattern of attacks by Iran on shipping and U.S. facilities in the Gulf region. “Iran appears to be pursuing a strategy of deliberate, calibrated escalation,” he wrote in an analysis on X. “The objective is not necessarily to trigger an all-out war, but to steadily increase the military, economic, and political costs of maintaining the blockade.” He said that Washington is faced with the dilemma that a limited response may encourage Iran to push further, while a stronger response risks accelerating the escalation that the U.S. is trying to avoid. “As long as the U.S. naval blockade remains in place and no agreement is reached, further escalation will become increasingly difficult to avoid,” he said. “There are two clear paths to de-escalation: a negotiated agreement or a U.S. decision to lift the blockade.” Iran renews attacks on American bases After Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran on Feb. 28 to launch the war, Iran regularly fired on American facilities and interests in neighboring Gulf countries, as well as energy infrastructure and other targets. In the attack early Wednesday on the Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait, the Iranian military fired at air defense systems and drone and missile launch platforms, according to a report on Iran’s state broadcaster. Kuwait’s military said that its air defenses had intercepted drone attacks and didn’t immediately report any damage. The Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry condemned the repeated Iranian attacks as “criminal,” saying that they threatened the country’s security and stability. During the war, Ali Al Salem Air Base has been struck at least 30 times by Iran, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area, according to an analysis by The Associated Press. The AP’s analysis used satellite imagery from multiple providers to help determine that Iran’s strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early-warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage. AP also spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or had firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment. Under questioning before a U.S. Senate committee Tuesday about damage to the Navy’s regional headquarters in Bahrain, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said he couldn’t offer a full damage assessment in Bahrain because “it’s a nonpermissive area for us to go.” He told a reporter months ago that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain.” Meanwhile, Bahrain’s Interior Ministry issued two alerts early Wednesday urging people to take shelter, followed by the “all clear” a short time later. The country’s military later said that it had intercepted a number of attacks from Iran, but gave no information on any damage or casualties. Conflict with Houthis in Yemen could stretch for months Saudi officials have briefed allies that the conflict with the Houthis could last for another six months, according to a diplomat familiar with the matter. The diplomat, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity, added that the kingdom in diplomatic talks is making the case that the military alliance working to restore the internationally recognized government in Yemen still must further set back the Houthis before it can begin credible talks with the rebel group. The Iranian-backed Houthis control a significant swath of Yemen, including the capital of Sanaa, and have made territorial gains along the Red Sea coast in the current conflagration. They’ve also rattled the kingdom with missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi infrastructure, including on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and energy infrastructure. The kingdom continues to make the case to allies that U.S. military support could help change the course of the war in the Saudi-led coalition’s favor, the diplomat said. But thus far, Trump has resisted the push from his ally for U.S. strikes on the Houthis.

articles.title: Mayor of US city with largest Muslim population calls El-Sayed's election 'an American story'
articles.summary: Sen. Abdul El-Sayed's historic win drew praise from Dearborn's mayor, who calls the first Muslim American elected to the Senate a truly American story.
articles.body: The mayor of the first Arab-majority city in the U.S., home to one of the largest Muslim populations per capita in the nation, told Fox News Digital Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s election to the U.S. Senate was "monumental." "It was monumental, and it's [truly] an American story where the brightest and best of us was elevated to one of the highest offices in the world — a member of the United States Senate — and where the people of Michigan elected an individual regardless of the direction in which he prays, but rather based on the direction in which he wishes to lead," Dearborn, Michigan, Mayor Abdullah Hammoud told Fox News Digital. "I think that is truly a beautifully American story." NYC'S MAMDANI SAYS ABDUL EL-SAYED'S SENATE VICTORY IN MICHIGAN 'MEANS SO MUCH TO SO MANY' Hammoud's comments followed El-Sayed’s Nov. 3 victory over former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan's high-stakes race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. With the win, El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat and former Detroit health director, became the first Muslim American elected to the U.S. Senate. In his victory speech in Detroit shortly after the race was called, El-Sayed took direct aim at the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). The pro-Israel lobbying group and its affiliates poured roughly $30 million into the August Democratic primary to back U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens against El-Sayed, and he thanked the group for the chance to "beat you twice." Celebrating his victory, El-Sayed also invoked the Arabic phrase "Alhamdulillah," which translates to "Praise be to God." ABDUL EL-SAYED DELIVERS MAJOR BLOW TO GOP IN MICHIGAN AFTER BRUISING SENATE RACE Throughout the campaign, El-Sayed faced repeated scrutiny over his rhetoric on Israel, concerns among some Jewish voters in Michigan and allegations of family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, claims El-Sayed rejected. He also drew criticism from fellow Democrats over his campaign appearances alongside controversial far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who previously faced backlash over incendiary remarks regarding the Sept. 11 attacks and Israel. Three days after his win, El-Sayed addressed the Arab America Foundation’s Connect Empowerment Summit in Chantilly, Virginia, just outside Washington, D.C., where he referred to Michigan as the "capital of Arab America." "I know we’re here in D.C., which, of course, is the capital of the United States of America. But Michigan is the capital of Arab America," El-Sayed said. During the speech, El-Sayed also pushed back against the attacks he faced on the campaign trail, saying opponents "wanted to make this a referendum on me and my name and my faith." ASRA NOMANI: EL-SAYED GLIDES INTO ROLE AS ROCK STAR OF THE HARD LEFT'S RED-GREEN ALLIANCE Hammoud, who became Dearborn’s first Arab American and Muslim mayor in 2022, explained to Fox News Digital what El-Sayed meant by calling Michigan the "capital of Arab America." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think he's just speaking to the idea that the largest concentration of Arab Americans happens to be in the city of Dearborn, just [as] you have so many other cities across America celebrating the unique demographic — sometimes the largest of X population residing within their city bounds — no different," Hammoud said.

articles.title: Bukele gets hero’s welcome from afar as thousands rally in Haiti after gang crackdown
articles.summary: Thousands marched in Haiti to thank Nayib Bukele for sending troops to battle violent gangs, prompting an emotional response from the Salvadoran president.
articles.body: Thousands of people in Haiti took to the streets Tuesday in a show of support for Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele deploying troops to the country to combat violent armed gangs. The demonstration unfolded as Haiti's Minister of Justice and Public Security, Patrick Pélissier, prepared to travel to San Salvador to discuss anti-gang strategies and ongoing troop cooperation. The president reflected on the moment in a post on X, sharing a video capturing a sea of people chanting, dancing and cheering in celebration. "I never expected anything like this. I hear you loud and clear. I love you too. We will triumph. God will give us victory," Bukele said. BUKELE WARNS HAITIAN GANG LEADERS THAT HIS FORCES WILL 'FINISH' THEM AS HE DID IN EL SALVADOR According to Reuters, some demonstrators carried signs reading "Long live Bukele" and "Down with the gangs," while others voiced their support for the Salvadoran leader. "Only a week of operation, we can see the path to change in Haiti. We say thank you to Bukele for all the help he gives us," demonstrator Claudy Mayas said. Another demonstrator said Bukele was providing Haitians with the one thing they had been waiting years for. "Four years ago, I could not go to Champs de Mars. I couldn't go to the south of Haiti," a demonstrator, also identified as Claude, said. "We don’t ask much of the government. We don’t ask for jobs. We need only security." ROBOT DOGS MOUNTED WITH RIFLES DEPLOYED IN ANTI-GANG STADIUM OPERATION IN HAITI Just two weeks ago, Bukele backed an operation involving devastating airstrikes that destroyed the headquarters of 400 Mawozo, one of Haiti's most powerful criminal gangs. The home of its leader, Lanmò San Jou, was also targeted in the operation, Bukele previously said. The direct military action marked a dramatic escalation in Haiti's fight against years of severe gang violence and insecurity. Bukele joined the mission after four Salvadoran members of the U.N.-backed anti-gang force went missing in a suspected gang ambush near Port-au-Prince on Oct. 18. At the time, Bukele sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti. EL SALVADOR-BACKED AIR ASSAULT DESTROYS HAITI GANG HEADQUARTERS AMID SEARCH FOR MISSING TROOPS While residents paraded through the streets in celebration, U.N. officials issued a statement Tuesday reminding leaders that anti-gang operations must prioritize civilian protection. "Security forces must strictly limit the use of lethal force to situations where it is unavoidable to protect life from an imminent threat and as a last resort," the agency said. According to the U.N., armed gangs control an estimated 80% to 90% of Haiti's capital and are expanding into surrounding regions. articles.title: What do Trump, Putin and Xi want from their Shenzhen meeting?
articles.summary: The US, Chinese and Russian leaders are to hold their first three-way talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
articles.body:
A three-way meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has begun in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, the first ever between the leaders of the world’s three most powerful militaries.

The meeting, which is taking place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, has drawn comparisons with the 1945 wartime Yalta conference at which the United States, United Kingdom and then-Soviet Union agreed on the post-war order for the world. But those powers had been allied during a world war. Analysts say the three men meeting now have arrived with very different goals, and that few concrete outcomes can be expected.

“It’s a summit of Trump’s ego, Putin’s tactics, China’s strategy,” Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera.

So what does each leader want from this meeting?

The trilateral meeting is taking place on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ summit, which China is hosting in Shenzhen over two days this week. Trump travelled to China after attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations ( ASEAN ) meeting in Manila.

The White House has said that Trump wants to discuss the war with Iran as well as a possible three-way agreement on nuclear armament with Xi and Putin. Trump has also stated he wishes to talk about the war in Ukraine, although Xi is understood to be reluctant to be drawn into what he views as a European matter.

The meeting comes as Trump’s ties with traditional US allies have come under strain. He has, at times, floated troop withdrawals from South Korea and cuts to assistance for Japan, while his administration continues to describe China as Washington’s main geopolitical rival.

Vuk Vuksanovic, a lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy at the Department of War Studies, King’s College, London, cautioned against viewing the summit as a new “carve-up” of the world order, however.

“It is a far cry from being a new Yalta,” he said. “In Yalta, you actually had the idea about how the world was going to look, and where the demarcation line would potentially be between the superpowers. We don’t have anything similar, not even the contours of that, in the making at this moment.”

At the Yalta Conference in February 1945, US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to shape the post-war order, agreeing on the division of Germany and setting the stage for Soviet influence over Eastern Europe.

Where do China-Russia-US relations stand?

There are competing interests at play here.

Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday, with Xi greeting him at the airport. This is their third in-person meeting since they paused their bitter trade war late last year. At its height, US trade tariffs on Chinese goods reached 145 percent, with China retaliating with tariffs of 125 percent on US goods, before a temporary truce agreed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, when tariffs were relaxed. Xi also agreed to pause new restrictions on exports of some rare earth metals which are crucial for manufacturing technology from smartphones to fighter jets. Soon after that, Trump relaxed restrictions on the sale of some Nvidia AI-related computer chips to China.

The truce has since been extended to January 10, 2027 to allow for broader trade talks.

China’s rare-earth mineral exports to the US are still about 75 percent below normal levels, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

A scandal over Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company accused of diverting Nvidia chips to China in breach of US export controls, has also strained ties, as has the recent scandal over Nvidia’s former CEO, Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs, including with a woman the US has accused of spying for China.

Beijing rejects all spying allegations as “baseless”, and Trump has said he does not plan to raise the issue at this meeting.

Expectations are low for a major thawing, however: Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, told Al Jazeera that a handshake without incident would be seen as a win.

Trump’s special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, have brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11, the first in direct format since February. The pair have visited both Kyiv and Moscow to promote these talks in recent days.

Days before they travelled to Moscow on Thursday last week, Trump said Washington and Moscow were close to a “big, beautiful agreement” covering not just Ukraine but “all of Europe”.

Trump’s rhetoric towards Putin has softened greatly in recent months, as it has hardened against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom he has publicly admonished for targeting Russian energy facilities, driving up the global cost of oil and diesel. Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to step down and has paused some sanctions on Russian oil, much to the anger of many in his Republican Party .

Some analysts are concerned that US negotiators may offer Russia concessions on NATO in return for peace, including pushing a deal that allows Russia to retain land it has seized from Ukraine in the past four years – a prospect that alarms European leaders.

China has become Russia’s top trading partner since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, weeks after the two had declared a “no limits” partnership.

At a summit in Beijing in May this year, Xi and Putin signed more than 40 cooperation agreements and hailed growing energy trade.

Russian oil exports to China rose 35 percent in the first quarter of 2026, according to a Kremlin aide. China has also ignored Western demands to stop supplying high-tech components to Russia’s weapons industry.

Chinese President Xi Jinping called for China and Russia to “lead and advance the trend towards a multipolar world” after holding talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

The two leaders also met on Wednesday in Shenzhen.

Putin addressed the summit after Xi. He described Western powers as “former hegemons” and said Europe was experiencing a “humiliating decline”.

Analysts say Trump is the leader most eager to walk away with something he can present as a “win” from this trilateral meeting.

Vuksanovic said Trump is coming to it “wounded domestically” following his Republican Party’s crushing defeat at the US midterm elections, which have seen the Democratic Party gain control of both US Houses of Congress. Trump’s legacy, Vuksanovic added, has been damaged by the war on Iran, particularly in light of Trump’s pledge not to drag the US into another “forever war” during his presidential campaign in 2024.

The deadlock that currently exists between the US and Iran has been described as a “ frozen war ” by observers.

“[Trump] hopes that he can get some quick-fix deal on something, at least, which he can then try to spin and sell to his base in the US as an enormous accomplishment,” Vuksanovic said. But he added that he doubts Trump could secure anything beyond “something very symbolic”, noting that the agenda of the meeting has remained opaque.

One issue Trump may push for is a trilateral agreement on nuclear armament. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) between Russia and the US lapsed in February. It was first signed in 2010 and caps US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.

Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty after it expired, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing. However, Xi is understood to be unenthusiastic about joining a treaty that China had no part in writing.

Lucas said Trump is there largely “for the photo opportunity”. But he drew a distinction between Trump and his administration, which he said wants to “regain their footing a little bit in terms of leadership” on China.

Washington’s China policy, Lucas said, has been “a disaster”. The administration launched a tariff war that saw duties climb as high as 145 percent, before Beijing retaliated by squeezing exports of rare earth minerals, forcing a truce.

“They’ve got to try to say: ‘Look, we’re leaders. Look, we have a firm policy on China, but one that’s not confrontational,'” he said.

That balancing act is complicated at home, Lucas added, with Republicans in Congress pushing for a tougher line on Beijing as the administration’s position weakens.

For Putin, the meeting is above all about the war in Ukraine and ending Russian isolation as a result of European and US sanctions.

“Putin and the Kremlin want cover for the invasion of Ukraine, because they’ve got some serious problems with it,” Lucas said. Moscow wants to keep the Trump camp on side, gain more Ukrainian territory and see Washington withdraw support for Kyiv, he added, while securing at least political backing from Beijing.

Lucas said Russia also wants to break “the notion that it’s isolated” after years of sanctions and the costs of a nearly five-year war that has not delivered victory. Putin is eager to prevent the US sanctions bill, which Trump has paused – and which would impose steep tariffs on Russia and on buyers of its goods, including China – from being implemented.

Vuksanovic said the optics alone, therefore, will be a prize for Moscow. After decades of complaining about US dominance, he said, Russia and China can now argue that “the power gap is not as great, so now we can sit at the table with the US”. That image of great-power status, he added, is “particularly appealing” to Putin.

Lucas added that Putin is unlikely to give up his leverage relating to Iran, and will resist offering Washington any binding promise that Moscow will not cooperate with Tehran.

For Xi, the host, the meeting is a chance to secure the space to pursue China’s long-term interests without interference.

“China wants the space to pursue its political, economic and military goals,” Lucas said. Beijing, he added, already has what it wanted in terms of recognition: “Now he’s on the same level with Trump and with Putin.”

What Beijing wants next, Lucas said, is no return to the tariff wars, no opposition to its alternative economic model, recognition of its primacy in rare earth minerals and technology, and no US pushback over Taiwan, which it regards as part of its territory.

China does not want anyone challenging its regional military presence, he said, including the Quad grouping of the US, Japan, India and Australia.

Vuksanovic described China as a rising superpower that is nevertheless “much more inward-looking” and focused on a vast process of internal reform. “They actually much rather prefer to be patient and to think long term, rather than to go for anything which is diplomatically grandiose,” he said.

He argued that China is “probably the biggest winner” of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, which have kept Washington distracted from the Asia Pacific. Beijing’s main worry, he said, is the risk of energy markets collapsing.

“Minus that economic risk, they’re still happy that the US is bogged down in two major wars which Washington does not know how to disentangle itself from,” he said.

Will this meeting change anything on Iran or Ukraine?

Observers are not expecting any sort of a breakthrough from this meeting.

On Iran, Lucas said the US administration would like Beijing to “privately urge the Iranians to make compromises”. But US-Iran talks remain stuck on whether to address the Strait of Hormuz and financial incentives for Tehran first, or its nuclear programme.

Vuksanovic said he is “very dubious” that China would take on a major mediating role. Beyond brokering the Saudi-Iranian rapprochement in 2023, he said, Beijing has preferred to be “diplomatically skilful rhetorically, without sticking out as a major conflict mediator”.

On Ukraine, Vuksanovic said Moscow sees the war as existential and believes it can win through attrition. Russia, he said, will not give up its minimum demands of full control of the Donbas and Ukraine renouncing its bid for NATO membership.

“I don’t think that this meeting will have any bearing on the outcome of the Ukraine war, which will not be resolved at a diplomatic table, but on the battlefield,” he said.

Lucas said Russia will instead try to keep Washington focused on what the Kremlin calls a Europe-wide security architecture, a framing that sidesteps a ceasefire, the territorial question and security guarantees for Kyiv.

Where Moscow and Beijing do agree, Lucas said, is in wanting the US to confine its ambitions of dominance to the Western Hemisphere. But he warned against seeing the summit as a carve-up among equals. “It’s much more a dynamic process where power is shifting, and where these leaders and their administrations are trying to preserve or even regain power,” he said.

What is the rest of the world hoping for?

Governments do not want Trump, weakened by the midterms, returning to a tariff war with China or disrupting their own economic ties with Beijing. The European Union faces a looming decision on its own economic relationship with China, he noted, while Canada, under Prime Minister Mark Carney, and the Gulf states are already recalibrating their approach.

“They would like a little bit of space themselves where they’re not having to respond to self-inflicted crises,” Lucas said. “So they’ll want Trump to behave.” They will also hope Putin is open to some pullback in Ukraine, and that China uses its power responsibly.

Vuksanovic said countries of the Global South will welcome the three powers talking, which fits their thinking on multipolarity. But they will also bring “a healthy degree of scepticism”.

“They will primarily observe whether there is any tangible outcome which impacts their own respective interests,” he said, from conflict resolution to the global economy, energy and new technologies.

articles.summary: "The View" co-host Whoopi Goldberg demanded Congress impeach HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. after the U.S. lost its measles elimination status Tuesday.
articles.body: ABC's "The View" co-host Whoopi Goldberg demanded that the incoming Democratic Congress impeach U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. after the country lost its measles elimination status Tuesday. The panel on Wednesday's show discussed the Pan American Health Organization announcing that for the first time in 26 years, the U.S. lost its measles elimination status after more than 5,400 confirmed cases were reported this year. The hosts largely blamed Kennedy for the outbreak, pointing to his past scrutiny of vaccines as a cause for the rise in cases, with Goldberg going as far as to hold him responsible for measles-related deaths. I don’t wanna say it, but I feel like he’s responsible for many people not making it. Get him gone, man!" When co-host Joy Behar remarked that members of President Donald Trump's cabinet could still remain in office for two more years, Goldberg doubled down on Kennedy's impeachment. "Start with this one!" Goldberg continued. "Start with this one, and then go to [Secretary of War Pete] Hegseth, and then go to the other ones, and get people in these positions who can actually do the damn job! We are tired of this! People are dying! Children are dying! Stop it! Impeach him!" CHERYL HINES SAYS 'THE VIEW' HOSTS JUST WANTED TO 'GRILL' HER ABOUT RFK JR, DIDN'T TALK ABOUT NEW BOOK In a comment to Fox News Digital, White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster defended Kennedy and said that the Trump administration has repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, citing an ABC News interview with Trump from April 2025. "President Trump and Secretary Kennedy have both stated that vaccination is the best way to prevent measles infections. In response to outbreaks, the President and Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country," Schuster said. Fox News Digital also reached out to HHS and ABC for comment but did not immediately receive a response. articles.title: Exclusive: ‘There was no monitoring.’ Sources say FAA had little oversight of work that led to nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: On the morning of last week’s historic nationwide ground stop, an FAA technician escorted a private contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communicatio...
articles.body:
On the morning of last week's historic nationwide ground stop , an FAA technician escorted a private contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control centers in south Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router.

The FAA technician believed his role ended when the contractor entered the facility. He went about his own work without knowing exactly what the L3Harris engineer was doing, according to two sources familiar with what happened in the room, and the union that represents FAA technicians.

Not long after it was replaced, that new router triggered a cascade of communications problems, flooding the FAA's aging network with data and leading the FAA to take the rare step later that day of issuing a full nationwide ground stop. About 3,500 planes were in the air when departures were halted for more than four hours while the agency worked to figure out the problem.

The details of how that router was installed and who was overseeing that work is now in dispute and emerging as a key point of tension in unraveling what exactly went wrong that day.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has defended the FAA's modernization process and insisted that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade "was monitored by an FAA technician" and that a risk assessment was done beforehand.

But sources who spoke to CNN dispute this characterization. The technician "was only there to unlock the door," one of them said.

"There was no monitoring," another source said.

That kind of hands-off arrangement, sources say, is a recent development and represents a stark change from how this kind of maintenance work was handled by previous administrations, when the FAA typically exercised far more oversight of contractors' work.

But in an effort to speed up and streamline the modernization of the nation's air traffic control system with $12.5 billion from President Donald Trump's "big beautiful bill," the administration diminished FAA oversight of this kind of work, the sources said.

In a memo dated March 2025, the FAA laid out some key changes to how maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, noting: "It is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay."

Under the policy change, the FAA shifted from receiving maintenance "requests" from its private contractors to receiving "notifications" of intended work, noting that "this work will proceed without FAA approval," according to the memo.

The memo does note that an FAA liaison will evaluate the "purpose, severity, criticality and impact" of the work, but the sources told CNN there are only a handful of liaisons nationwide processing thousands of notifications.

"So what level of oversight are they really doing?" one of the sources said.

As a result, the L3Harris contractor at the center of Friday's outage showed up with just a few days' notice and conducted the work without any meaningful oversight from the agency, according to the sources and the union.

The March 2025 memo "laid the groundwork for what happened last Friday," the source said.

"They're not requesting to go out anymore. They're just notifying and going and then they're doing the work," the source said. "And that circumvents the operational risk management aspect where the technician before who works for the government could say, no, no. You can't do that right now."

Elizabeth Doherty, a spokeswoman for the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union that represents FAA technicians, told CNN the technician's "orders were to simply let the contractor in the building," that he "had no direction to help or assist in any way," and that "no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade."

CNN asked the FAA about the discrepancy over whether an FAA technician was or was not providing real time oversight of the work.

"There is a lot of information that we're trying to track down. So things have been changing," FAA spokeswoman Hannah Walden told CNN by phone. "It could have been a misunderstanding or whatever. So I'm not saying one way or the other right now. I just am saying we're trying to provide information as we get it."

In addressing the changes laid out in the 2025 memo, Walden denied oversight has been reduced, saying the policy change "does not change oversight at all. It changes the priority of the work that needs to be done."

After this story published, Walden sent an additional statement, seeming to contradict what Bedford said publicly on Tuesday about the technician monitoring the upgrade.

"The FAA escort is responsible for providing the L3Harris technician access to and from the building. Because it is L3 equipment, the escort is not there while the technician is doing work," she said in the statement.

The episode underscores the complications that can arise over a communications system that is operated by the federal government yet is owned by a private company, in this case L3Harris, whose telecom network serves as the communications backbone for the nation's airspace.

It also comes as Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is asking Congress to approve another $50 billion to upgrade the nation's air traffic control system even as lawmakers question how the billions allocated last year were spent.

L3Harris declined to provide any details in response to CNN's questions.

In a statement to CNN, the company said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel."

The policy change laid out in the March 2025 memo didn't come out of nowhere. The sources familiar with what happened before the ground stop said a chronic, yearslong shortage of FAA technicians as well as the Trump administration's push for speed helped propel it forward.

The result, they believe, was less oversight of the contractor on Friday and a much slower recovery, as the FAA struggled to pinpoint the source of the problem.

L3Harris notified the FAA on November 9 that it planned to carry out maintenance, replacing a router, at a remote FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, with work set to begin at 9 a.m. on Friday, November 13, one of the sources said.

Four days after the notice, the L3Harris worker arrived.

Even the time of day the work was scheduled raised eyebrows, given it was at a time of heavy air traffic. The sources say FAA technicians were not consulted about the best time to carry out this work at this facility.

By that Friday afternoon, the new router was connected and the L3Harris contractor had left the site with no idea of the chaos that was beginning to unfold, the source said.

Hours later, FAA technicians got a call telling them to return to the site to escort the L3Harris engineer back into the facility. The agency scrambled to find the closest available staff to let him in. Hours had passed between the time the engineer had left and the time he returned to retrieve the router, the source said.

A former FAA technician told CNN that, for agency technicians, checking in with air traffic controllers before leaving a site is standard practice. It's not clear if the L3Harris engineer took this step.

"As a technician, anytime when I was out there … and I did anything, anything at all to the equipment before I left, I would call up the TRACON or the center or the tower, whatever controllers that had the services that I was providing on that equipment. And I would say, 'I'm getting ready to leave. Everything look good? Everything okay? You got everything?' They'd be like, 'yep,'" the former technician said. "It's just a practice that you do."

In the immediate aftermath of the ground stop, Duffy was sharply critical of L3Harris, making a point of calling them out in his public remarks.

"We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job," Duffy said during his Saturday press conference. "Many of our contractors, many or our partners, they take our money and they provide really poor service to us. Full stop."

Yet by Tuesday, Bedford sounded a different tone toward L3Harris.

At a news conference, Bedford described the L3Harris contractor who replaced the router as a "highly trained certified engineer, former Air Force veteran, I'm told a generally competent guy doing the work that he has done dozens and dozens of times before."

Asked what oversight the FAA provides when contractors work at FAA facilities, Bedford also said, "There is a comprehensive risk management process with every installation. And that installation happens whether it's with a contractor or with an FAA employee."

Days earlier, Duffy had defended the timing of the work, pointing out that it was at a remote location. He said he didn't expect the kind of impact seen last Friday at "smaller locations."

articles.title: Miami court convicts US-Haitian pastor over 2021 assassination of president
articles.summary: Prosecutors accused Christian Emmanuel Sanon of seeking to replace then-Haitian President Moise.
articles.body:
A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship has been convicted in the United States on charges stemming from the assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moise, following a nearly eight-week trial in a federal court in Miami.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon, 68, was found guilty on Wednesday on all eight charges, including conspiring to kill the Caribbean nation’s president, who was shot dead in his home on July 7, 2021.

Prosecutors said in court records that the scheme to kill Moise, 53, included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programmes that were intended to help businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic.

They said South Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moise and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing.

Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moise, but said the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill the president and maintained his innocence throughout the trial.

He was arrested in Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, days after the assassination. According to a report by local police seen by the Reuters news agency, when officers searched his residence, they found eight vehicle registration plates, 19 passports and 12 mobile phones, as well as 30 boxes of ammunition and 12 pistol holsters.

Moise’s widow, Martine Moise – a key witness in the trial – was flown to Florida for treatment for bullet wounds she sustained in the attack. She has now registered as a presidential candidate for Haiti’s 2027 general election , the first in more than 10 years.

Sanon, who remains in federal custody, showed little reaction as the jury verdict was announced. He faces up to life in prison and is set to be sentenced on February 10.

His attorney, Zeljka Bozanic, said the defence team was disappointed and would file an appeal at the appropriate time. Prosecutors declined to comment after the verdict.

US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination, and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.

A new list of indictments released by US prosecutors in September included four people whose names were redacted.

Seven more people have been charged for their roles in facilitating the funding of the assassination plot and helping those responsible evade justice after the killing, including Vitel’homme Innocent, a gang leader tied to the kidnapping of 17 US and Canadian missionaries later in 2021. He has yet to be arrested.

Those still to face trial include Joseph Felix Badio, a former government anti-corruption official whom other suspects’ defence lawyers have accused of masterminding the operation, and 17 Colombian former soldiers flown in from Haiti in September.

Assassination plunges Haiti into turmoil

Haiti has not had a president since authorities said a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers impersonating US Drug Enforcement Administration agents killed Moise and injured his wife in a night-time raid on their home outside Port-au-Prince.

A series of transitional governments followed, as armed gangs, widely believed to be aided by corrupt politicians, seized control of much of the capital and surrounding regions.

The United Nations Human Rights Office documented 4,595 people killed in armed violence between January 1 and October 31 this year.

The situation has caused economic, security and humanitarian crises, forcing nearly 1.5 million people to flee their homes, according to the UN.

articles.title: BJP leader's son run over by flower-showering bulldozer at Akhilesh Yadav's Gorakhpur 'rath yatra'
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A 12-year-old boy was killed after being run over by a bulldozer during a Samajwadi Party (SP) roadshow led by party supremo Akhilesh Yadav in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 12-year-old boy was killed after being run over by a bulldozer during a Samajwadi Party (SP) roadshow led by party supremo Akhilesh Yadav in Uttar Pradesh's Gorakhpur, news agency IANS reported.Former UP CM Akhilesh Yadav received grand 'bulldozer welcome' as he held PDA 'rath yatra' in Yogi Adityanath's bastion, Gorakhpur.The deceased, identified as Aryavardhan Singh, was a resident of Rajdhani village in Chauri Chaura. His father is a local BJP leader.The incident took place in the Koodaghat area during the SP's Rath Yatra, officials told IANS.According to the boy's father, Omkar Singh, the bulldozer was showering flower petals on the rally when it hit his son. He alleged that Akhilesh Yadav's convoy had already moved ahead when the bulldozer, which was approaching at high speed, struck the boy from behind.Speaking to news agency IANS, Omkar Singh said, "Around 2pm, when Akhilesh Yadav's convoy passed, my son was going to pick up his sister from Kendriya Vidyalaya. While he was crossing the road, Akhilesh Yadav's convoy had moved ahead.""A flower-showering JCB was following the convoy at a very high speed so that flowers could be showered on Akhilesh Yadav from behind. During that time, my son was crossing the road when the JCB ran over him. He died on the spot," he added.The impact of the collision reportedly flung Aryavardhan towards a road divider, leaving him with a severe injury to the back of his head. He later succumbed to his injuries.The incident triggered a sharp reaction from the Uttar Pradesh BJP, which alleged negligence in the conduct of the roadshow and criticised the behaviour of SP supporters during the procession.In a statement, the UP BJP said, "In Gorakhpur, SP supporters, in their frenzy to welcome Akhilesh Yadav, took the life of an innocent 12-year-old child! The child died a painful death after being hit by a JCB during the PDA chariot procession -- the result of SP supporters' rowdiness and irresponsible behaviour.""This is what they're like while out of power; imagine the havoc they'll wreak once they come to power! Should we call them SP supporters or hooligans? Is a show of power more precious to them than an innocent child's life?" it added.An investigation into the incident is under way. Further details are awaited.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Far from Trump-Putin meeting, Europe to count cost of Ukraine’s defence
articles.summary: European leaders set to meet in Berlin as Kyiv faces a 25 billion-euro ($27.4bn) financing gap next year.
articles.body:
As US President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China, European leaders are due to gather in Berlin to agree on funding for Ukraine’s defence and press Washington’s visiting envoys for a European role in Russia-Ukraine peace talks.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting the so-called Coalition of the Willing summit on Thursday alongside French President Emmanuel Macron and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. More than 30 leaders are expected to attend, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The summit agenda includes long-term security guarantees and continued military and financial support for Ukraine. Zelenskyy has said air defence will be his immediate priority as Kyiv enters a winter with the threat of Moscow’s drone attacks looming.

Trump administration envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected, according to media reports, to meet Ukrainian officials and Europe’s newly formed negotiating team in Berlin. The team includes France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, plus European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

Washington has backed European participation in the next round of talks, but Moscow has yet to agree.

The impasse could put Ukraine’s main financial backer on the sidelines of talks over its future, as European Union countries are set to make even steeper commitments.

The European Commission on Wednesday proposed an additional 45 billion-euro ($49.3bn) loan for 2027, with up to 25 billion euros ($27.4bn) for military aid and 20 billion euros ($21.9bn) for budget support. That follows a 1.71 billion-euro ($1.87bn) payment on Monday under an existing EU loan for drones, ammunition and air defence.

Even if the new loan is approved, it would leave a 25 billion-euro ($27.4bn) financing gap next year.

Zelenskyy said the US envoys had promised to brief Kyiv on Trump’s discussions in China, where he is meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin.

The Berlin summit gives European negotiators a chance to agree on what they want from the next round and put it directly to Trump’s envoys, just days after a public disagreement between the transatlantic partners emerged in Brussels.

At Tuesday’s Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting at NATO headquarters, Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s undersecretary for policy, argued that some Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia had done little to slow Moscow’s military advances and that attacks on civilian infrastructure may have hardened Russian resolve.

In a swift backlash, German Federal Minister of Defence Boris Pistorius called the assessment “quite a stupid thing” and pointed to Russia’s repeated attacks on Ukraine’s electricity and heating infrastructure. London was quick to align with Berlin, with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting arguing that Ukraine should decide how to fight and that its long-range strikes had weakened Russia’s military capabilities.

After a nine-month hiatus, US, Ukrainian and Russian officials resumed talks in Abu Dhabi last week. Witkoff and Kushner then met Putin in Moscow and said Europeans would join the next round, despite Moscow throwing cold water on the idea.

Within Europe, newfound energy has emerged with the prospect of the bloc joining negotiations, with EU leaders agreeing in Dublin last week on a team.

Sharon Hudson-Dean, a senior fellow with the Center for European Policy Analysis, told Al Jazeera that “success” in Berlin would mean firmer commitments to Ukraine’s immediate defence and its 2027 budget, as well as closer alignment between Washington and European capitals.

European leaders, she said, are wary of US announcements and Russian intentions and want a say in decisions that will affect their security, budgets and markets.

“Washington should leave Berlin recognising that Europe will shoulder much of the financial and security burden of implementing any settlement, and as such, needs a seat at the table,” Hudson-Dean said.

With Europeans likely to bear many of the costs of security guarantees, sanctions and Ukraine’s path to EU membership, she said, they want to be “in on the takeoffs, not just the crash landings”.

Ahead of the Berlin summit, European allies pledged more winter aid for Kyiv and outlined plans to deliver fighter jets and air defence missiles, as Zelenskyy urged them to release Patriot and IRIS-T interceptors from their stocks, offering to replace them with missiles Kyiv has on order.

The Ukrainian leader also said Ukraine needed 40 more F-16s.

In response, Germany and Norway each announced $300m for the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a NATO-coordinated programme that buys US weapons for Ukraine. Their joint package includes Patriot missiles.

The UK, Denmark, the Netherlands, Finland, Belgium, France, Sweden, Lithuania, Estonia and Portugal all reiterated or pledged further funding for Ukraine in the lead-up to the Berlin summit.

Poland will be represented on Europe’s negotiating team, but Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Friday that Warsaw would put no additional money into PURL at this stage. Bulgaria, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia have indicated they will opt out of the next round of EU financing.

Despite elections in Hungary that ushered in a more EU-friendly leadership, Budapest continues to oppose military assistance for Kyiv.

Kinga Koranyi, an assistant professor at the University of Wroclaw who studies Hungarian politics and EU governance, told Al Jazeera the idea that Hungary should “stay out of the war” remains widely shared after years of politicisation under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s Fidesz party, leaving direct funding for Kyiv unpopular.

Years of lost access to EU funds over rule-of-law disputes have also made Budapest cautious about new spending, she said, as the cost of the war with no end in sight continues to mount.

articles.title: Los Angeles' abandoned $1.2 billion Oceanwide Plaza towers became covered in graffiti after construction stopped in 2019; crews have now cleaned about 250 balconies as buyers plan an $850 million revival
articles.summary: A building adorned with art is often considered beautiful, but in downtown Los Angeles, an unfinished real estate project became a canvas that was not
articles.body: A building adorned with art is often considered beautiful, but in downtown Los Angeles, an unfinished real estate project became a canvas that was not appreciated for the city's aesthetic. Once envisioned as a luxurious address featuring high-end residences, a hotel and retail spaces, Oceanwide Plaza eventually became known for walls of graffiti that turned an ambitious real estate project into one of the city's most notorious eyesores.After years of neglect, interest in the project has been revived. Crews have removed graffiti from approximately 250 balconies across the three buildings, clearing an important hurdle in plans to revive the unfinished $1.2 billion development. The prospective buyers, KPC Group and Lendlease, plan to complete the development as originally envisioned with an investment of $850 million.From an ambitious dream to three abandoned skyscrapersOceanwide Plaza is located in downtown Los Angeles, at the intersection of Crypto.com Arena and the Los Angeles Convention Center. It was designed to be a major addition to the city's skyline. The three-tower development was being built by Beijing-based developer Oceanwide Holdings. The developer group had invested approximately $1.2 billion into the project by 2019 when the group ran out of money, bringing construction to a halt. The development was approximately 60% complete but the project never saw completion. The complex was planned to bring together luxury residential apartments, a hotel, shopping spaces and other lifestyle amenities, creating a lively destination in the heart of downtown LA.How the towers became a giant graffiti canvasThe abandoned buildings attracted a very different kind of attention in early 2024. Graffiti artists began accessing the unfinished structures and covering their exterior balconies and windows with colourful spray-painted designs. Slowly, the three skyscrapers transformed into enormous vertical canvases.The graffiti stretched dozens of floors above the streets, with some drawings made as high as 54 storeys. The striking colours made the buildings difficult to miss, particularly against the otherwise conventional downtown skyline.As reported by the LA Times, the building also became a place from where BASE jumpers parachuted from the towers. A performance artist also filmed himself balancing on a narrow slackline stretched between two of the buildings.Eventually, the towers became known as the 'Graffiti Towers,' a nickname that was perhaps more memorable than the original project's name.250 balconies cleaned in a challenging operationOn November 12, 2026, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass celebrated the removal of graffiti from approximately 250 balconies across Oceanwide Plaza's three towers. The cleanup was not an easy task for the workers. They had to tackle graffiti at considerable heights, sometimes operating from window-cleaning platforms suspended from above. Much of the paint had to be removed by hand using a biodegradable cleaning solution.The cleanup was also a condition imposed by the city on the prospective buyers before the property sale could move forward. Mayor Bass had insisted that the visible graffiti be addressed before further restoration work began. According to the Los Angeles Mayor's Office, the removal marks an important step towards restoring the property and revitalising downtown Los Angeles.An $850 million comeback is on the cardsThe prospective buyers, KPC Group and Lendlease, plan to complete the development as originally envisioned, with 504 residential units, a luxury hotel and a shopping centre spread across the three towers.According to the Los Angeles Times, the developers estimate that another $850 million will be required to finish the project. The bankruptcy sale is valued at approximately $517 million and is expected to close in January 2027, subject to the necessary financing arrangements.There are also hopes of making the property presentable ahead of the 2028 Summer Olympics, when Los Angeles will welcome visitors from around the world. Plans reportedly include a massive electronic sign on the building's facade. The developers are still working on securing construction financing, so the revival is not quite guaranteed yet.Los Angeles' bigger plan to bring downtown back to lifeAlong with the announcement about the cleanup of Oceanwide Plaza, Mayor Karen Bass revealed other developments under the Downtown LA Revitalization Plan. The plan aims to make the neighbourhood safer, busier and more welcoming, not just by restoring abandoned buildings but by bringing everyday life back to its streets. The plan includes modernising and expanding the Los Angeles Convention Center, which is expected to attract more than 186,000 visitors and generate over $400 million in economic impact.There is also a new Vacant to Vibrant programme to turn empty shops into active small businesses, alongside increased police patrols and better public transport safety through Metro Ambassadors. The city is also encouraging businesses to return, with Banc of California leasing 40,000 square feet of office space downtown. Community groups, residents and local businesses are being brought into the process, too, with dedicated working groups and park advisory boards.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Sandown should show uniqueness in culture bid - head judge
articles.summary: Sir Phil Redmond visits Sandown as part of a whirlwind tour of the shortlisted towns.
articles.body:
An island town should show what makes it unique in a bid to be crowned Town of Culture 2028, the competition's head judge has said.

Sir Phil Redmond visited Sandown on the Isle of Wight on Wednesday as part of a a whirlwind tour of the British towns all bidding for the inaugural title.

It is one of 15 to have made the shortlist in the Small Towns category.

Speaking to the BBC during the informal visit the Grange Hill and Brookside creator said: "We want people to take a breath really and look at their particular place and say 'what is unique about this particular place, why do we like this place, why do we want to celebrate this place?'."

Launched in October 2025 by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), all towns outside of Greater London without city status are eligible to apply with three finalists chosen.

The winner will receive £3m and will be given the Town of Culture designation for one year, while the two runner-ups will receive £250,000.

Sir Phil, who chairs the independent advisory panel for the UK Town of Culture 2028 competition, said it has been "fantastic" to visit the shortlisted towns.

"It's really just for me to come and see the place [and] also see the people who've been involved with the bid who are going to deliver the bid," he said.

Nearly 400 places from across the country entered the landmark competition.

Sir Phil said Sandown making it to the shortlist is "in itself is a great achievement".

Sir Phil added: "I think I've witnessed that today they've already discovered the real prize and that's when people come together and start building partnerships or strengthening partnerships and they all start working to a common purpose."

Sandown received £60,000 to develop its full bid which will be assessed by the independent judging panel.

One finalist will then be selected from each category with the overall winner being announced early next year.

articles.title: Parents live in fear paedophile nursery worker harmed their children
articles.summary: A number of parents whose children were looked after by Nathan Bennett call for CCTV in nurseries.
articles.body:
Parents are calling for mandatory CCTV in nurseries after a worker who looked after their children was later exposed as a paedophile.

Nathan Bennett was jailed in February for multiple counts of sexual abuse, including two counts of rape, against five boys at Partou King Street nursery in Bristol. His crimes were discovered after a CCTV review.

Bennett previously worked as an apprentice for 18 months at another nursery in the Somerset area - which the BBC is not naming – which does not have CCTV.

A number of parents whose children went there said they lived in fear about what could have happened to them at the nursery. The government said a panel was examining the use of CCTV in nurseries.

Warning: This story contains distressing details

Bennett's victims at Partou King Street nursery were two and three years old at the time of his offences. In February 2025, concerns were raised over his behaviour with the children, specifically a group of five who the prosecution said he would "favour".

He was suspended from the nursery after CCTV of him putting his hands down a boy's trousers was reviewed.

There is no evidence he committed any offences while he worked at the Somerset nursery, or that there were safeguarding failures there. Avon and Somerset Police said it had not identified grounds to warrant a criminal investigation at the site.

Det Insp Lucy Forde, who led the investigation into Bennett's crimes, previously told the BBC she feared only a fraction of his crimes could be proven.

"He's worked in childcare and has had access to children for a number of years," she said.

"My worry is there will be other victims that we haven't been able to identify, that are too young to understand what's happened to them," Forde added.

After learning of Bennett's offending, a number of parents whose children went to the Somerset nursery shared their worries about what could have taken place. The BBC has changed their names to protect their children's identities.

Rachel, whose children attended the nursery, said she became suspicious of Bennett after witnessing him being overly tactile with her child in her opinion.

The BBC has seen messages from the time exchanged between Rachel and her partner, in which concerns about Bennett's behaviour were discussed, describing him as "weird".

They discussed raising concerns about him and eventually complained to management about their son being repeatedly left in soiled nappies and being sore.

Rachel said they eventually asked for their child to be moved away from Bennett's care.

"My son was always on Nathan's lap - there would be times where I would see him stroking him on his arm, kissing him on the forehead or cheek," she said.

"There was something inside me that knew straight away that's not right," she added.

Rachel said she saw Bennett taking her child into the nappy changing area alone with the door closed on one occasion.

"I came to pick up my son and I could hear him crying - the changing room door was closed so I waited for a while.

"Nathan came out with him, alone, and said 'I'm not sure what's up with him, he never seems to like his nappy being changed','" she said.

Rachel said healthcare professionals had since referred her child for an assessment by specialists who deal with cases of sexual assault.

If you have been affected by this story or would like support then you can find organisations that offer help and information at the BBC Action Line .

James, whose children attended the nursery at the same time, said he witnessed Bennett being "too physical" with children.

"Most times I went to pick up my children he was holding a child on his lap or making physical contact with a child," he said.

"More often than not, the child looked like they were trying to get away, but he was holding them there. I didn't see other nursery staff with children on their lap," James said.

He said he verbally complained to nursery managers about Bennett.

"I told them I had observed Nathan being physical with children – in my opinion too physical.

"Their response was 'isn't it great how cuddly he is?'," he said.

Bessie Martin, a former colleague of Bennett's at Partou King Street nursery in Bristol, previously told the BBC she had also witnessed him holding children on his lap.

"I would see a child try to wriggle away or stand up and walk off, but he'd say 'sit here and we're going to read a book'," she said.

She became a whistleblower and reported her concerns about Bennett to senior management at Partou.

During his trial it emerged parents had raised concerns to the nursery in the six months before he was caught.

James said news of Bennett's conviction led him to worry about the worker's behaviour when he was an apprentice.

"I was concerned that he didn't become a predatory paedophile when he moved to the nursery in Bristol – I believe he was always a predatory paedophile," he said.

James said CCTV in nurseries should be a "minimum requirement".

"If I was to go through choosing a nursery again, it's something I'd need to have in place," he said.

Another parent, Helen, said she wanted to see mandatory, actively monitored CCTV and stronger safeguards, including higher qualification requirements for staff and strict enforcement of two-person working.

"Mandatory CCTV should not be a problem – especially in places with extremely vulnerable people, where it's most needed," she said.

"Something positive needs to come out of such a horrendous thing," she added.

Helen said the uncertainty of not knowing if anything could have happened had led her to "read into everything".

"Any comments [from my child] about nursery now, you don't know how to interpret them.

"My child will sometimes start a conversation saying, 'mummy, I didn't tell you this thing that happened at nursery' and I start shaking every time she says it," she added.

Katie and John Meehan, whose daughter Genevieve was killed at a nursery in Stockport in 2022, have also been campaigning for mandatory CCTV in nurseries.

CCTV footage showed nursery worker Kate Roughley tightly swaddling nine-month-old Genevieve, strapping her to a beanbag and leaving her unattended. She died of asphyxiation.

John Meehan said that - while CCTV was not a "silver bullet" - use of it could "identify unsafe practices" or provide evidence for the regulator and police when harm occurred.

"For parents entrusting their precious and vulnerable children to a nursery, the confidence and reassurance these safeguards can provide are vital," he said.

The Department for Education said it had strengthened recruitment and safeguarding requirements at nurseries.

It said this included full criminal record checks for staff working closely with children, checks on references before a hire, new safeguarding training and clear processes for staff to raise concerns.

Allegations or concerns that a staff member has harmed a child or is unsuitable to work with children should be reported to the council's Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO).

The nursery where Bennett was an apprentice said one concern was raised following Bennett's conviction, which the LADO confirmed did not meet the threshold for investigation.

The nursery was rated Outstanding by Ofsted at the time of Bennett's employment. The regulator told the BBC there had been no concerns raised during Bennett's employment at the nursery.

In an email sent to parents following Bennett's conviction, the nursery said Bennett was employed as an apprentice and subject to a high level of supervision.

A man who worked at the nursery at the same time as Bennett said he had not noticed any suspicious behaviour but was concerned staff could sometimes be left to work alone, even if they had no previous childcare experience.

"I had never worked in early years or childcare before," he said.

"The chances of being alone when changing a nappy were quite high.

"The door wasn't always open when [Bennett] was changing nappies," he added.

A member of staff who worked at the nursery after Bennett had left, said she had often felt overwhelmed with the number of children she was given to look after.

While she said whistleblowing policies and safeguarding procedures were clearly explained at the nursery and people were encouraged to report anything that did not sit right, she added that complaints she raised about having too many children were not addressed, and she eventually quit her job.

"It was horrendously overwhelming and eventually I couldn't do it anymore," she said.

Rachel said the impact of knowing her child went to a nursery where Bennett was working would be "lifelong".

"The moment I found out he had been convicted confirmed how I had felt that year about Nathan Bennett," she said.

And although she cannot do anything about the lack of CCTV at the Somerset nursery, she said mandatory video monitoring could deter other potential offenders - or provide proof for other families after a crime had happened.

"It didn't deter Nathan Bennett, but without it he would be free to continue committing these crimes," she said.

articles.title: Newcastle art students get sneak peek of new city studio
articles.summary: The Quayside Studios have facilities for photography shoots and to record music and podcasts.
articles.body:
Arts students have been given a sneak peek of a new creative content studio they hope will support their careers.

Newcastle College photography and music students had a chance to try out facilities at the £1.8m Quayside Studios, funded by the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority (NEMSA), with support from the city council.

G Thompson, 29, is doing a photography degree and said it was great to try out a professional set-up.

"We don't really have anything like this in the city. There's a few [studios] that you can rent for like £500 a day, which doesn't allow working class people to take advantage of it, which I don't think is very fair."

As well as a photography suite, the studios offer spaces to record music and podcasts.

Music performance student Zoe Hai, 22, got to work with other students on a new song in the space.

"I think it's amazing to have something so well equipped, something so nice that is also so local that we can get to easily instead of having to go for away to a big city."

The studios, which are in the converted Grade II listed Coronation Buildings, are officially set to open in 2027.

Photography lecturer Alan Thoburn said people would often have to move to London or Newcastle to get opportunities in the industry, but he was hopeful the new facility would change that.

"It's great to have it, you get a sense of things happening in Newcastle and the North East - more photography, more opportunities and more jobs for people in the industry."

North East Mayor Kim McGuinness said the region had cultural ambitions and wanted to offer local talent a place to hone their skills.

"On top of that it provides a space where those people who've already made it - the Sam Fenders and the Jades of the world - can make albums on the banks of the Tyne with that incredible view and show those young people they can do it too."

articles.title: North Yorkshire caterer went bust 36 hours before couple's wedding
articles.summary: Lorraine and Mark Norwood say they were contacted by Baba Ganoush less than two days beforehand.
articles.body:
When Lorraine and Mark Norwood's wedding caterer pulled out less than 36 hours before their big day, the couple were left in "absolute shock and horror".

In an email sent just before midnight on 1 October this year, their provider, Baba Ganoush, said they were "heartbroken" to say they had taken the "devastating decision to cease trading with immediate effect" and would be unable to fulfill their commitment.

"It was complete disbelief at first," Mark said, after they opened the message on the Friday morning, "then shock, then anger that we were let down so badly".

With less than 24 hours to go, and having already paid £7,000 for a three-course meal and canapes for their 76 guests, they were left scrambling for a replacement.

Mark said: "They must have known for quite some time that they were in financial difficulty.

"They could have given us a heads-up or warning but obviously chose not to and just took the money and ran instead."

While the couple were able to secure an alternative caterer at the last minute, they had to borrow £3,000 from a relative to cover the extra cost, and said they were not hopeful of getting their money back.

Since their wedding, they said they had learned that in the weeks before Baba Ganoush went bust the North Yorkshire-based firm's directors, Matthew and Ashley Hyde, had set up a new catering company.

The BBC found that company, initially called Hyde Hospitality but now going by the name Marjoram Yorkshire Limited, had been registered on 30 August.

According to Companies House, Baba Ganoush - Dining By Matthew Hyde Limited remains "active", though it has 10 County Court Judgments (CCJs) against it, which, as of October, totalled more than £43,000.

In a statement to the BBC, Ashley Hyde said: "We fully recognise the upset, disruption and financial consequences experienced by the affected couples, particularly those who received very little notice, and we sincerely apologise for the distress caused.

"There were other significant factors involved which we are not currently in a position to discuss publicly while the relevant matters are being examined."

Since Lorraine and Mark came forward, the BBC has spoken to other customers, former employees and suppliers who all say they have encountered difficulties with Baba Ganoush.

Sophie, who did not want the BBC to use her surname, said she had paid Baba Ganoush £4,000 to cater for her wedding in June 2027, before the company went into liquidation.

She said that after the company went bust she was contacted by Marjoram Yorkshire asking if she wanted to transfer her existing contract to the new company and saying if she did "100% of all monies" would be honoured.

However, when she declined, she said she had been told that to get her money back she would have to pursue a claim through the firm's liquidators, as the company "was not in a position to give refunds".

She said she was hoping to be able to make a claim through her credit card company.

Other brides-to-be have accused Baba Ganoush of being "pushy and persistent" by demanding payment up front, offering "deals" if they paid off more of their balance quickly.

Ashley Hyde told the BBC she was assisting with wedding insurance claims and was "willing to discuss" other potential resolutions.

She said the company had made it clear to all affected clients that they were under no obligation to enter into a new agreement with Marjoram Yorkshire.

Former Baba Ganoush office manager Georgina Schorah said she had had to take time off for stress in August 2025 after bailiffs - looking to collect unpaid rent for a previous premises - forced their way into the company's York office while she was working alone.

She said she had contacted Ashley and Matthew Hyde asking them to come to the office, but, despite saying they were on their way, they did not turn up.

She said she was subsequently made redundant and spent six months pursuing the company for £2,000 in outstanding wages.

The 29-year-old said she had been forced to take out a loan to cover her expenses and had only received payment after she contacted the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service (Acas).

She described the company's finances as "chaotic" and said there had been a number of complaints from couples over the quality of the food and a lack of staff.

Georgina alleged the firm would "always try and get away with not refunding them for as long as possible" and accused them of "taking on bookings when knew they were in severe financial difficulty and did not have the staff".

She claimed the firm "managed to go for so long and carry on for so long because the staff were the ones that were picking up the pieces".

Ashley Hyde said Baba Ganoush "strongly disputes" any suggestion it knowingly continued to accept or retain bookings with the intention of not fulfilling them, but the circumstances surrounding the cancellations "were not purely financial".

She cited "operational circumstances" and other factors that the company was "not in a position to discuss publicly".

Another former staff member, Max Haynes, 21, said he spent almost a year chasing the company for £800 he was owed, and ended up taking Baba Ganoush to an employment tribunal.

He claimed that on one occasion, while awaiting payment, the company had sent him a screenshot which appeared to show that a bank transfer had been made, but he said the money did not arrive in his account.

The BBC has also seen screenshots from Georgina, showing similar images which suggested she had been paid, though she said she had not.

Max, from York, said: "I know she [Ashley] would lie to almost everyone who would ask her, where's my money? She'd give some excuse.

"The judge at the tribunal ruled I had won, but it eventually went to bailiffs who went round to the premises twice before she eventually paid me.

"It was a horrible experience to go through. I'd spent hours working for my money to pay for uni - rent, food, travel expenses - money is already tight as a student."

Responding to Max's claims, Ashley Hyde said: "We strongly dispute suggestions that certain employment matters were ignored or left unresolved for prolonged periods.

"Some employees entered into formal settlement and confidentiality agreements with us as part of earlier negotiated resolutions of employment matters."

During his time working for the Hydes, Max said he had witnessed kitchen staff attempting to source ingredients or equipment for weddings hours before the event because suppliers had not been paid.

Adam Gough, who runs Wharfeside Hire, based in York, said it was like "torture" waiting for payment, saying he was still owed £18,000 by Baba Ganoush for 22 weddings.

Like Max and Georgina, he said in around July 2024 he was sent copies of banking records showing that he had been paid, but said no money arrived in his account.

When asked about Adam's account, Ashley Hyde said she "categorically and unequivocally denies" sending misleading images of bank transfers and said the non-payments were due to technical issues with her bank, Tide.

Adam, 45, said he had eventually taken Baba Ganoush to court "but they didn't even turn up" and had been "handed a CCJ in its absence".

He said when he had told them he planned to speak publicly about the issues, the Hydes had said they would sue him for slander.

He said they were "very good at getting rid of bad things online", adding: "They're like dogfighters when they hit the bottom."

He said he was not notified when Baba Ganoush liquidated, despite being owed money

When asked if he thought he would ever see his money, he replied: "I am waiting for their next steps."
