articles.title: Increase in direct cremations since Covid-19 pandemic
articles.summary: A 2026 Cost of Dying Report found direct cremation was now chosen for around one in five funerals.
articles.body:
Funeral directors say there has been an increase in direct cremations, with no mourners in attendance, since the Covid-19 pandemic.

Brian Ugalde, whose firm of funeral directors has worked in Cornwall for 135 years, said non-attendance had become more acceptable since the lockdowns when families were not always allowed to attend.

He said: "A funeral is a ceremony...a farewell, a celebration... it is for for those left behind," he said. But, he said, direct cremation came after Covid when "the model became acceptable and practical", as well as being cheaper.

SunLife's 2026 Cost of Dying Report found direct cremation was now chosen for around one in five funerals in the UK.

The report said, in the majority of cases, the deceased had requested or arranged a direct cremation themselves before their death.

In 86% of those cases, families decided to hold their own celebration of their loved one's life at a later occasion.

Andrew Judd from The Association of Funeral Directors said families did not always realise exactly what was included when they bought a direct cremation plan.

"The average cost of a direct cremation at the moment is £1,628," he said.

"So that's the cost of the person that you've lost being collected from where they died, being cremated somewhere in the country and you having the ashes delivered back to you, that's all it is."

If you were to have an attended funeral service, that can range from £4,200, but you have a funeral with that."

John Ware from Walter C Parsons funeral directors in Plympton suggested people talked to loved ones before buying an unattended cremation plan so their family knew what to expect.

"If they talk to their local funeral director there is probably an option that sits somewhere between a direct cremation and a completely traditional funeral which would suit the need of both parties, in terms of keeping the cost lower, but also having a service that the family can attend to reflect on that person's life."

Plymouth's The Park crematorium, which opened in 2024, has recently reduced the cost of direct cremation, citing lower prices offered by other crematoria and national companies.

Graham Smith, head of bereavement, registration and coroner services at Plymouth City Council, said national providers could use crematoria in other parts of the country meaning not everyone was cremated in their home city.

"In my view if you live in Plymouth, if you work in Plymouth, why would you use a national provider?"

VAT, the cost of wood for coffins and fuel price increases have all added to the cost of traditional funeral services. But people the BBC spoke to in Plymouth had mixed views on direct cremation.

Andrew Statton said he had not previously heard of direct cremation but added: "My wife died seven years ago of cancer and we had the ashes and then had a memorial service afterwards, so it makes no difference does it?"

Ann Roberts said she would consider a direct cremation because it would save her family money and they could "decide what they want to do". She added: "If you don't talk to your family, they won't know what you want."

But Pam Brinkhurst said she preferred a more tradition funeral. "When you get cremated or buried the family are there. It's a much better send off."

Phoenix Elson agreed: "I would rather pay the extra money and for my son to actually be there to celebrate my life".

Simplicity is one of the national companies offering direct cremation and said "our nationwide network of crematoria helps us keep fees competitive".

They added: "Giving customers more choice, including the option to be cremated locally rather than having their loved one transported across the country to secure the lowest fee, is a positive development for consumers and the sector as a whole in the Plymouth area."

articles.title: Sheffield's Penny the peahen finds fame in her Hillsborough home
articles.summary: The bird was first spotted in Hillsborough in June, with her antics followed by hundreds on social media.
articles.body:
A Sheffield suburb's residents have welcomed an inquisitive peafowl into their community after the bird set up home in local streets and gardens.

The peahen was first spotted near Hillsborough Park in June, with the "serial trespasser" regularly flying between the same few streets.

Dubbed Penny by the locals, a Facebook page reporting her antics through photos and videos has more than 850 followers.

Nicola Cowan, who set up the social media account, said: "I think she's different and quite sassy, the local cats were trying to catch her and had no luck.

"There were people from rescue groups who came and no one was successful, so I think she became a bit famous."

Hillsborough resident John Highfield recalled the moment he first met Penny.

"I was minding my own business when there was a knock on our back door," he said.

"A man is there who I think is trying to sell us something, and this guy says, 'Do you know you've got a peacock in your garden?'

"You don't expect to see that in your own garden on any afternoon."

Although peahens have rather muted colours when compared to the vivid plumage and dramatic tail feathers of the male peacock, Highfield described Penny as "quite lovely".

"She has these little tuft of feathers but she has incredibly big claws, she looks like an ostrich from the ankles down," he said.

"They are big, you wouldn't want to get on the wrong side of her."

Michelle Nicholson's back garden is a regular haunt for Penny, according to the resident.

"She comes several times a day and sits at the top of our carport, especially in the summer," she said.

"She pecks away at the petals and plants sometimes, but apart from that she doesn't do any damage."

Nicholson has taken to feeding the peahen dog biscuits as a treat.

"Now she ignores all the bird seed and just eats them," she said.

"I just find her really interesting and she's quite tame."

She believes Penny roosts nearby at the top of a set of tall trees, but no one is sure how she came to settle in the S6 area of the city.

However, one peafowl expert does have a theory.

Suzanne Chambers, who runs a peafowl farm in Worcestershire, said: "They are lazy flyers who fly up and down.

"If they're scared they will not look where they are going and get lost."

The bird could have been "scared by a dog or a fox or some banging from a building site", the expert said.

Chambers believed Penny could become a long-term resident of Hillsborough if looked after properly.

"This will be her new home now," she said.

"She'll be settled, but probably be a bit lonely as they are sociable flock birds.

"She will definitely need to be fed, ideally game feed, wild bird seed or meal worms - something high in protein.

"She'll need water too to help build her condition."

articles.title: Gipsy Lane flooding in Swindon alarms elderly resident
articles.summary: Brian Reynolds, 78, says flooding on Swindon's Gipsy Lane regularly reaches his front door.
articles.body:
An elderly resident who has had four heart attacks in two years says he is worried ambulance staff "won't be able" to get him out of his house in an emergency because water floods right up to his front door after heavy rainfall.

Brian Reynolds, 78, has lived on Gipsy Lane in Gorse Hill, Swindon for 31 years and said the drains had "persistently" flooded since he moved there.

"I am so fed up. Enough's enough. They don't understand the stress I am under," the pensioner said.

Jake Chandler, Swindon Borough Council cabinet member responsible for flooding, said the authority had launched a "full flooding investigation" and structural works would take place within six months.

"It's the worst I've seen it, my drain is solid," said Reynolds. "[Flood water] comes up two of the three steps to my front door and to the top of my wellington boots."

Gipsy Lane sits on the edge of an industrial estate and at the bottom of a hill, meaning silt and industrial fragments also enter the drainage system.

Reynolds also told the BBC he was a carer for his terminally ill daughter and being able to leave his house to get to her in an emergency was difficult.

The pensioner also pointed out the "soakaways" on the opposite side of the road were not connected so they did not take the water away, adding to the build up.

In the past the council added the 10ft (3m) soakaways which "allow for some alleviation of flood water", but they are now also blocked, Chandler added.

Chandler, who is also deputy council leader, told the BBC it had "taken steps to make sure the drains and soakaways were unblocked", but in the medium to long term it needed to address the source of the flooding.

He added: "It is because of how the road is shaped and because of potential blockages in gullies and culverts nearby."

Local councillor Princia Fernandes said she was concerned for multiple elderly residents including Reynolds, as well as parents trying to get their "kids out the door to school" and go to work.

"It's not a one off, it's been a problem for years. I've seen the gully cleaning but there's more to this than the gullies, the pipes' size is smaller and needs to be assessed," Fernandes said.

She also said it was a matter that needed to be discussed with neighbouring businesses to find the "root cause" and a "long-term solution".

Chandler said: "We've launched a full flooding investigation so we'll be going in and examining every gully and culvert and checking where there could be potential blockages.

"It's one thing to go periodically and clear out the street gullies, but if they are blocked 10 or 100 ft down - which isn't visible to human eye - you're only dealing with the issue at the surface," he added.

articles.title: How online mocking of antique gates in Staffordshire led to a Harry Potter TV opportunity
articles.summary: Joel Paxton says online criticism helped put his antique gates in front of the right audience.
articles.body:
What started with online criticism ended with an unexpected call from the team behind the new Harry Potter TV series for an antiques dealer.

When Joel Paxton posted a video of a set of gates on social media, he attracted hundreds of comments from people who disliked them.

But among the almost one million people who watched the clip was a set designer, working on HBO's new Harry Potter series.

Soon afterwards, Paxton was contacted about the gates and found himself getting a behind-the-scenes glimpse of one of television's most anticipated productions.

"We had an interesting set of gates that came through the door, and I'd say they're quite a unique piece," said Paxton, who runs Rustique Living in Sandon, Staffordshire.

"We did a little video on that, and it just blew up for some reason."

Among the online comments were reactions ranging from "yuck" to "disgusting", with some social media users questioning why anyone would want to buy the gates.

The attention turned out to be exactly what the business needed.

"One of the set designers got in touch and wanted that set of gates for the new Harry Potter series," Paxton said.

The TV adaptation, which is due to debut at Christmas, stars Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

Paxton started Rustique Living while studying for a business degree at Keele University.

What began in his parents' front room during the Covid pandemic has since grown into a shop specialising in unusual antiques and furniture.

"Everybody's after something unique, and finding these unique pieces is always tricky, but when you do, you know you've dropped on something really interesting," he said.

The gates certainly caught people's attention.

The video received nearly 950,000 views on Facebook alone before attracting interest from the Harry Potter team.

Paxton later drove the gates to London himself and was given a glimpse behind the scenes of the secretive production.

"It's an interesting experience because you're not allowed certain access into certain places because you can't get spoilers," he said.

The Harry Potter project is not the first production to buy from Rustique Living.

Paxton said the company had also supplied items to programmes including The Traitors and was increasingly receiving inquiries from television and film productions.

"Recently it's been pretty much every week," he said.

The Harry Potter connection has also proved good for business.

"A lot of people have come in and said they've seen the video of sending things to Harry Potter," Paxton said.

"People come in off the back of that and go, 'I wouldn't mind something from the shop that sells things to Harry Potter.'"

articles.title: Netanyahu’s last stand and the dangerous politics of survival
articles.summary: Facing political oblivion, Netanyahu is playing a high-stakes game that could push Israel towards violence and chaos.
articles.body:
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the weeks since Israel’s October 27 election to launch a series of attacks on his opponents, and has called into question the legitimacy of the vote’s result.

The longtime Israeli leader is likely on his way out of power – as long as the country’s opposition, led by Gadi Eisenkot, can form a viable government.

That may involve leaning on parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, and Netanyahu has taken the opportunity to use that to tarnish the reputations of the Arab parties, and baselessly accuse them of cheating in the elections.

The environment that Netanyahu has helped generate has led to right-wing protesters threatening civil war, and critics have also accused him of deliberately fomenting war with Iran to retain office.

Separately, the Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency, led by Netanyahu’s ally David Zini, reportedly sought permission to tap the phones of five Arab lawmakers over suspected foreign interference, and to have politicians who are Palestinian citizens of Israel arrested on election day, requests the attorney general rejected.

Opposition leaders including Yair Lapid and Joint List chief Yousef Jabareen said the measures were evidence of an “attempted coup”. Meanwhile, law enforcement officials are said to be investigating whether the prime minister’s office itself fabricated the allegations of vote-buying.

For analysts and a number of Israel’s politicians, Netanyahu’s actions reflect an overriding determination to stay in power, or, failing that, engineer a government that is reliant on the support of him and his allies.

Netanyahu faces numerous threats to both his legacy and even his freedom that, without the kind of influence he has wielded as prime minister, could prove far-reaching.

Calls for a state inquiry into Netanyahu and his government’s failings in the run-up to the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel have persisted for almost as long as the genocidal war Israel launched on Gaza in response. Those calls have grown more urgent following a series of reports suggesting that Netanyahu had been personally warned by senior Egyptian and Emirati officials about a potential attack. Establishing a state inquiry also featured prominently on the legislative slate of the parliament’s new session last week.

Similarly, both the war in Gaza and the constitutional crisis triggered by Netanyahu’s attempts to weaken judicial oversight over the government have provided useful cover against the corruption charges he has faced since 2019. Accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases, Netanyahu has seen his trial, running since May 2020, repeatedly delayed by his duties as prime minister. If found guilty, Netanyahu could face a prison sentence of up to a decade.

“Netanyahu is behaving like a wounded animal,” said Israeli analyst Ahron Bregman, of King’s College London. “For him, losing the elections is not just a political but also a personal matter, not least because of his corruption trial, which could result in him being sent to jail. Losing the premiership is losing his shield. Hence, for Netanyahu, nothing is off the table.”

The chance of political violence in Israel has increased. In the days after the election, right-wing protesters gathered outside Eisenkot’s home, warning him not to form a government with the Arab-led parties, and calling him a “traitor”.

And in a letter shared publicly, Rabbi Gedalia Axelrod , a former head of Haifa’s rabbinical court, evoked the religious edict of din rodef, the “law of the pursuer”, the same principle invoked by Yigal Amir to justify his killing of former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in 1995 over the Oslo Accords agreement with the Palestinians.

“The longer it takes for Eisenkot to form a government, the higher the risk of political violence becomes,” said Ofer Cassif, a member of parliament representing the left-wing Hadash party. “Netanyahu is willing to do anything, and I mean anything, to stay in power. He’s a psychopath. People on the right talk about civil war, and I’m not ready to discount that … Netanyahu built a cult around him, and it may easily raise arms against his rivals.”

It remains unclear what, if any, immediate legal consequences Netanyahu may face for his alleged efforts to undermine the legitimacy of the election.

Aides accused of passing false information to the police on the eve of the election could face criminal scrutiny , while Shin Bet chief Zini could see both his agency’s independence and his own position fundamentally undermined by allegedly participating in efforts to subvert the democratic process.

“Netanyahu battles for his survival and doesn’t care if those around him disappear into oblivion, but he might not succeed this time,” said Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow at Chatham House. “He doesn’t care about them, or even his political legacy. All he cares about is survival, about fighting for the next day and trying to cling on, no matter what the cost.”

articles.title: In 1986, Ted and Ruth Baum bought a Joan Mitchell painting for $65,000; on November 16, 2026, the same artwork sold at Sotheby's in New York for $19.3 million, nearly 300 times its original price
articles.summary: An artwork purchased for $65,000 four decades ago has now fetched more than $19 million at auction, offering a striking illustration of how artistic
articles.body: An artwork purchased for $65,000 four decades ago has now fetched more than $19 million at auction, offering a striking illustration of how artistic vision, collecting instincts and time can transform the value of a painting. Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest (1960), once acquired by American collectors Ted and Ruth Baum, emerged as the star attraction at Sotheby’s in New York on November 16, 2026. The painting sold for approximately $19.31 million, almost 300 times its original purchase price, becoming the headline lot in a landmark auction dedicated to the couple’s extensive art collection.Joan Mitchell painting leads the Baum collection auctionThe sale took place as part of Sotheby’s Vision: The Extraordinary Collection of Theodore and Ruth Baum Evening Auction. According to Heni News, the Mitchell painting achieved a price 60 per cent above its $12 million low estimate. The work also carried a guarantee, providing a level of financial security ahead of the auction.Its remarkable performance underscored the continued appeal of Mitchell's work in the international art market. The painting had previously changed hands twice before reaching the auction block as part of the Baum collection.Another notable result came from Roy Lichtenstein’s Two Paintings: Sleeping Muse (Study) (1983), which sold for $3.78 million against a low estimate of $1.5 million. Heni News reported that the work, also backed by a guarantee, had been traded eight times previously.A collection valued at more than $100 millionThe Mitchell painting was among more than 130 works assembled by Ted and Ruth Baum, whose collection is estimated to exceed $100 million. As reported by The Art Insider and ARTnews, Sotheby's is presenting the collection through multiple auctions rather than offering it all at once.Around two dozen works featured in the November 16 evening sale, with additional pieces scheduled for a November 17 day auction. The remaining works will appear in different Sotheby's sales over the following year, although their final number and individual estimates have not yet been disclosed, the report adds.Before the auction, Rothko and Ruscha works were among the leading lots, each carrying estimates of $10 million to $15 million. Mitchell's painting was valued at approximately $12 million, while works by Burri, Fontana and Warhol were estimated between $4 million and $6 million.The Baums' journey as art collectorsTed Baum, a pioneering figure in American cable television, and Ruth Baum, an interior designer, began building their collection in the 1970s. Their interest initially centred on modern drawings and watercolours, with purchases including works by Fernand Léger and Pablo Picasso.According to ARTnews, their collecting ambitions evolved significantly in 1983, when they acquired an untitled 1967 Rothko painting on paper featuring red and orange tones. The purchase marked a turning point towards contemporary art and eventually led them to artists such as Mitchell, Sam Francis, Hans Hofmann, Lichtenstein and Wesselmann.Their later acquisitions reflected an equally strong interest in European abstraction. These included Lucio Fontana's Concetto Spaziale, Attese (1960), purchased at Sotheby's London in 2000, and Warhol's The Scream (After Edvard Munch) (1984), acquired in 2006.A legacy extending beyond the auction roomThe Baums' influence extended well beyond collecting. They supported cultural institutions and philanthropic initiatives across the communities where they lived, including New York, New Jersey, Southampton and Palm Beach.The Norton Museum of Art in West Palm Beach houses the Ruth and Theodore Baum Gallery, which displays part of their collection. The couple also supported the museum's contemporary art programme and contributed works by artists including Dale Chihuly and Leo Villareal. They were additionally associated with New York's Guggenheim Museum and the Parrish Art Museum.Ted Baum died in 2021, while Ruth Baum passed away in 2026, just months before the collection's major auction presentation.As part of the sale, Sotheby's is also taking selected highlights on an international exhibition tour, with presentations planned in London, Hong Kong, Los Angeles, Paris and New York, as reported by The Art Insider and ARTnews.The $19.3 million Mitchell result is therefore more than an exceptional auction achievement. It offers a glimpse into the legacy of two collectors whose decades-long commitment to art has now become part of the market's history.Images Courtesy: Sothebys, The Art Insider, and Joan Mitchell FoundationYou use AI every day. articles.title: Why is Pete Hegseth strengthening US military ties with Venezuela?
articles.summary: Hegseth’s new military deal with Venezuela raises questions about US influence, regional security and Maduro’s removal.
articles.body:
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced a new cooperation agreement with Venezuela’s interim government to facilitate military cooperation between the two countries.

The Pentagon chief’s announcement came during an unannounced visit to Caracas on Wednesday. The US says the agreement will help fight drug trafficking and improve security in the region. Venezuela says it will help strengthen its military without compromising its sovereignty.

But why is an agreement happening now, and what does each side stand to gain?

What is the new US-Venezuela military agreement?

The US and Venezuela have agreed to strengthen military cooperation in several areas, including joint training, intelligence sharing, military equipment and border security.

Hegseth met Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez and Defence Minister Gustavo Gonzalez Lopez in Caracas. He said the agreement would allow the two countries’ armed forces to work together to combat drug trafficking and armed groups operating in Venezuela.

Rodriguez described Hegseth’s visit as an extraordinary step in relations between the two countries.

She said renewed military cooperation would help improve troop training, modernise equipment and give armed forces access to new technologies.

Her government said the country’s armed forces, known as the Bolivarian National Armed Forces (FANB), would benefit directly from the agreement.

However, the full terms of the agreement have not been made public, including details of how the two countries would carry out joint military operations.

Why is the US strengthening military ties with Venezuela?

The Trump administration said closer military cooperation with Venezuela will help fight drug trafficking and armed groups, and improve security in the region.

Hegseth said the agreement should help Venezuela regain control of areas where armed groups and drug trafficking networks operate.

But political analyst Carlos Pina said the timing of the visit is important, particularly after the Democrats won the midterm elections in the US.

“I think many of the things happening between the United States and Venezuela are closely related to the November 3 election results,” Pina said.

He explained that the Democrats have already said they aim to increase scrutiny of US foreign policy towards Venezuela, including the agreements reached with Caracas during 2026, after US forces abducted then-President Nicolas Maduro and took him to New York. The US has since, in effect, taken control of Venezuela’s oil industry — the country has the world’s largest oil reserves.

Pina also pointed out the recent attempt to impeach Hegseth. “I think this Hegseth visit also falls within that framework, to get ahead of what will be the debate in the new US Congress.”

On November 10, the House of Representatives voted 211-204 against impeaching Hegseth for now, but Democrats could try again after January, with their new majority in the House.

The November resolution against Hegseth, introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, included eight articles of impeachment related to the US-Israel war on Iran, military strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats and the January operation that ousted Maduro from power.

Massie said Hegseth ordered an act of war against Venezuela without congressional authorisation. He argued that the operation went beyond arresting Maduro on drug trafficking charges and was also intended to give Washington control over Venezuela’s oil reserves.

“Secretary Hegseth executed unlawful orders effecting the removal of the President of a sovereign nation, placed boots on the ground, conducted preparatory bombardments, inflicted substantial casualties, and subsequently caused regime change, each of which constitutes acts of war,” Massie said in the impeachment resolution.

Pina believes Hegseth’s visit is partly aimed at defending Trump’s policy in Venezuela before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

“Hegseth goes to Venezuela, which is probably one of Trump’s few foreign policy successes, to show the American public that the plan they are carrying out in Venezuela benefits US national interests,” he said.

Why is Delcy Rodriguez cooperating with the US?

Rodriguez and her government welcomed the agreement, saying it will help strengthen the country’s forces and improve its training and access to technology.

Venezuelan officials have also stressed that the cooperation must respect the country’s sovereignty and constitution.

But analysts say the agreement may also signal Rodriguez’s efforts to remain in power following Maduro’s ousting.

“The simple answer is that they want to remain in power as long as possible,” Phil Gunson, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera.

He said Rodriguez’s government faces considerable pressure from Washington. “If they decline to cooperate, they have been told they will suffer the same fate as Maduro, or worse.”

He also pointed to Washington’s financial leverage over Caracas.

“The US currently controls most of Venezuela’s foreign earnings, in the form of revenue from oil sales , and can cut off the funds whenever it wishes,” Gunson said.

Since Maduro’s ousting in January, revenue from Venezuelan oil sales has been deposited into US-controlled accounts, with Washington supervising the release of funds to Caracas.

According to a Department of State report released on November 12, more than $12bn from Venezuela’s oil and other natural resources passed through these accounts between January and September.

The US government said nearly 99 percent of the money had been disbursed mostly to individuals and businesses in Venezuela through commercial banks. But the agreement means Caracas depends on Washington to approve the release of money from these accounts, potentially giving the Trump administration tools to put pressure on Rodriguez’s government.

Pina described the Venezuelan government’s approach as “a calculation of survival”.

“They are capable of yielding in certain areas to the US government, as long as their hold on government is not affected or threatened,” he told Al Jazeera.

Pina also said Rodriguez was trying to buy time, particularly as Democrats prepare to take control of the US Congress in January.

“She gains time,” he said, suggesting that greater congressional scrutiny of Trump’s Venezuela policies could eventually give Caracas more room to negotiate.

What could the agreement mean for Venezuela’s military?

One of the key questions, say analysts, is whether closer cooperation with Washington could lead to changes within Venezuela’s armed forces, many of whose senior officers served under Maduro.

Gunson said much would depend on Washington’s intentions.

“Will Washington seek to reform the security forces, whose leaders it has accused of drug trafficking, human rights abuses and collaboration with Colombian guerrillas and other armed groups?” he said.

He also explained Venezuela’s military is not in a position to resist US influence.

“In its current state, the military as an institution is not in a position to resist US influence, for good or ill,” he said.

But he explained that some senior officers could try to sabotage the process if they feared prosecution or losing their positions.

Separately, Venezuelan Defence Minister Gonzalez Lopez also issued his first statement since taking office.

He said the new relationship follows the “painful events of January 3”, when US forces removed Maduro from power.

Gonzalez Lopez said military cooperation with Washington would follow Venezuela’s constitution and respect the country’s “sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity”.

He also stressed that Venezuela’s armed forces would retain control over their own leadership, command and operations.

There is no clarity on the terms of the agreement.

But Pina said the agreement seems to focus on limited military cooperation, particularly operations against armed groups and drug trafficking networks along the Venezuela-Colombia border.

Pina said the two countries could carry out joint military operations, including air raids against armed groups operating in the area.

But he believes Venezuela’s military will be reluctant to give the US a much larger role.

“The Venezuelan armed forces are not going to concede beyond that,” he said.

Pina argued that Washington needs a stronger military presence in Venezuela if it wants to maintain its influence over the country’s political transition, particularly because armed forces remain under the governing party’s control.

What does the agreement mean for Latin America?

The agreement could affect other countries, particularly neighbouring Colombia, which shares a long border with Venezuela.

Several Colombian armed groups operate on both sides of the border, including the National Liberation Army (ELN), which has been fighting the Colombian government for decades.

Pina said the joint military operations could weaken these groups and reduce their ability to operate across the border.

However, on Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella had rejected a US proposal to allow joint military operations on its territory.

But De La Espriella denied the NYT report, saying Colombia wanted to strengthen military cooperation with Washington, although the presence of foreign troops would require congressional approval.

Hegseth also rejected the report, calling it “totally false”.

Gunson said Trump sees Venezuela as a major success and as a model for US relations with Latin America. But he said the results of the midterm elections could change how governments in the region respond to Washington.

“Governments in the region that seemed bound to fall into line with the US hemispheric security policy may start to think again,” Gunson said.

Pina also believes the agreement with Venezuela could raise concerns in other Latin American countries, including Mexico, about the possibility of US military operations on their territory.

“I think what happened with Nicolas Maduro marked a before and after in Donald Trump’s regional security policy,” Pina said.

He argued that the January operation showed Washington was prepared to use military force to pursue its interests, even when such actions could violate international law.

But Pina questioned whether the agreement represents a long-term change in US policy towards the region, or is primarily a political response to the recent attempt to impeach Hegseth.

articles.title: Florida pastor is convicted of charges related to assassination of Haitian president
articles.summary: A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted of U.S. charges arising from the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse, a killing that plunged the Caribbean nation into deep turmoil.
articles.body: MIAMI (AP) — A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted Wednesday of U.S. charges arising from the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse, a killing that plunged the Caribbean nation into deep turmoil. Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on all charges including conspiring to kill Moïse, capping a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced eight charges, the most serious being conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States. Sanon, who remains in federal custody, showed little reaction as the jury verdict was announced. He faces up to life in prison and is set to be sentenced next Feb. 10. Prosecutors declined to comment after the verdict. But Sanon’s attorney, Zeljka Bozanic, said the defense team was disappointed and would file an appeal at the appropriate time. Haiti has been without a president since the assassination Haiti has not had a president since authorities said a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a nighttime raid at their home on July 7, 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule. Federal prosecutors said at trial that South Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The prosecutors said Sanon was their initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. They also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging there for himself and others. Sanon had acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but said the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse. Born in Haiti, Sanon moved to the U.S. as a teenager. He testified that he has worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the Midwest. Prosecutors said South Florida was a hub for plotting against Haiti’s leader Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from U.S. government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid-19 pandemic, according to court records. U.S. prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences. The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in South Florida with a former Haitian senator and several U.S. businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies — Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU — for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators. CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said. By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their backing to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian Supreme Court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive. Sanon was once scheduled to be tried with four other men Sanon had been previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were ultimately convicted last May of conspiracy in the assassination. But Sanon’s case was subsequently separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons. At the earlier trial, Arcangel Pretel Ortiz, Antonio Intriago, Walter Veintemilla and James Solages were found guilty of conspiring to kill or kidnap the country’s elected leader and of providing material support for the plot. They were also convicted of violating the U.S. Neutrality Act and also face possible life sentences. They await sentencing. Separately, in late September, 18 suspects arrested in the case were extradited from Haiti to the U.S. Suspects who were in the Caribbean nation awaiting trial included 17 former Colombian soldiers and Joseph Badio, a former Haiti Ministry of Justice employee who was part of an anti-corruption unit. Badio, considered a key suspect, was arrested in Haiti in October 2023 after more than two years on the run and is currently in U.S. custody. His Miami-based attorney, William Barzee, didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment from The Associated Press. A general election in Haiti is scheduled next year for a new president. Candidates include the widow of Moïse, a respected economist, a well-known prosecutor accused of multiple summary executions and a former president accused of drug trafficking and sponsoring gangs.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: US President Donald Trump was seen helping Chinese President Xi Jinping on an escalator at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit
articles.body: NEW DELHI: US President Donald Trump was seen helping Chinese President Xi Jinping on an escalator at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's Shenzhen, in a moment captured in a video shared by the White House.The video, posted by the White House rapid response account on X, showed Trump assisting Xi as the Chinese leader stepped onto the escalator. During his meeting with Xi, Trump praised their relationship and said he would urge China to purchase more American agricultural products.“I'll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” Trump said.Xi described relations between Washington and Beijing as “generally stable and improved” during Trump's presidency.“The efforts you have made are there for all to see and will go down in history,” Xi said.Trump also met Putin, describing the Russian president as “my friend” and saying, “Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start.”The meetings are taking place against the backdrop of tensions over the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear weapons, trade and artificial intelligence. articles.title: US lawmakers want Trump to press Xi over wrongfully detained Americans, political prisoners
articles.summary: Senior US lawmakers have urged President Donald Trump to raise the cases of wrongfully detained American citizens and other political prisoners with
articles.body: Senior US lawmakers have urged President Donald Trump to raise the cases of wrongfully detained American citizens and other political prisoners with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their scheduled meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday.The appeal was made by House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, Values Action Team Chairman Robert B Aderholt and Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC) Co-Chairman Chris Smith, according to a press release issued by the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).The lawmakers urged the Trump administration to make the release of people detained on political grounds a priority in its talks with Beijing.They cited the release of Pastor Ezra Jin in July as an example of successful diplomatic engagement by the Trump administration. However, they said several other religious leaders, activists, journalists and prisoners of conscience continued to remain behind bars in China.In a joint statement, the lawmakers said that freedom of religion, speech and association were universal rights, but accused the Chinese Communist Party of continuing to deny these freedoms to innocent people.They pointed to the case of Pastor Ezra Jin, who spent nearly nine months in prison for leading a church. While he has been released, several other pastors, religious believers and journalists remain imprisoned, they said.The lawmakers also raised concerns over the imprisonment of Hong Kong pro-democracy media tycoon Jimmy Lai, 78, who was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his role in running the newspaper Apple Daily. They described the sentence as effectively a death sentence for a man of his age and said the American people had not forgotten his case.They also highlighted the case of pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong, who turned 30 while in prison and was recently handed an additional 10-year sentence. The lawmakers said they would continue to push for the release of both Lai and Wong.The statement also called for the immediate release of two American citizens, Youlin Chen and Min Zin, whom the lawmakers described as "wrongfully detained" scholars. They were arrested on allegations of endangering China's national security while conducting academic research.Other prisoners of conscience mentioned in the statement included Gulshan Abbas, a retired Uyghur physician; Christian pastor Gao Quanfu and his wife Pang Yu; members of Pastor Ezra Jin's Beijing Zion Church; and Uyghur scholar Ilham Tohti.According to the press release, Gulshan Abbas went missing in September 2018, days after her sister and Uyghur rights advocate Rushan Abbas publicly spoke about the persecution of Uyghurs. The lawmakers called for her release.They also raised the cases of Pastor Gao Quanfu and his wife Pang Yu, who remain detained over their Christian faith. Members of Beijing Zion Church are also behind bars following the October 2025 crackdown in which Pastor Ezra Jin was arrested.The lawmakers further highlighted the case of Ilham Tohti, a Uyghur academic who received the European Parliament's Sakharov Prize in absentia in 2019. He has remained in prison since his arrest and life sentence in 2014, the press release said.The Select Committee on the CCP also noted that both the US House of Representatives and Senate had passed resolutions calling for the release of American citizens wrongfully detained in China and other prisoners of conscience.The lawmakers reiterated their appeal to Trump to raise these cases directly with Xi and press for the release of those detained on political and religious grounds. They said the freedom and welfare of prisoners of conscience should remain a key priority in US engagement with China.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: North Korea expanding uranium enrichment facility, UN nuclear watchdog says
articles.summary: North Korea can produce both highly enriched uranium and weapons-grade plutonium at its facilities, according to IAEA.
articles.body:
North Korea is expanding a nuclear facility for enriching uranium, according to the head of the United Nations nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

An existing facility at the Yongbyon nuclear centre has been further expanded in the last couple of months, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said on Wednesday.

This comes as US President Donald Trump expressed his eagerness to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un while he is in Asia for an APEC leaders’ summit in China .

“Since mid-September 2026, a further extension to the original Yongbyon enrichment facility has been under construction with the new extension externally complete by late October 2026,” Grossi said in a statement to the IAEA’s board of governors.

“The ongoing expansion of the DPRK’s uranium enrichment program remains extremely worrying,” he added, using North Korea’s official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

Pyongyang has not allowed IAEA inspectors into the country for years. The IAEA, nevertheless, keeps watch on North Korea’s nuclear facilities, including through satellite imagery and open-source information.

North Korea has called its Yongbyon complex “the heart” of its nuclear programme. Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon.

North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui last week stressed that possessing such weapons was “the strongest guarantee” of his country’s sovereignty. Choe rejected the recent demand for North Korea’s complete nuclear disarmament by the Group of Seven (G7) economically powerful democracies.

Disarmament of the global nuclear weapons arsenal is likely to be a topic at the trilateral meeting between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in Shenzhen, at Trump’s request.

While Trump expressed interest in meeting with Kim, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said no meeting was yet scheduled with the North Korean leader during Trump’s Asia visit. However, he added that the president is prepared to begin a new dialogue with Pyongyang .

articles.title: Noida couple pays Rs 25.2 lakh for a 150-sq-yard plot to build dream house in 2021; builder delays possession and sells land to another buyer for higher price, consumer commission orders refund with 6% interest
articles.summary: NOIDA: The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission of Gautam Buddha Nagar has directed Mohali-based Bajwa Developers Ltd, through its managing
articles.body: NOIDA: The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission of Gautam Buddha Nagar has directed Mohali-based Bajwa Developers Ltd, through its managing director Jarnail Singh Bajwa, to refund Rs 25.2 lakh with 6% interest from the date of filing of the complaint, April 9, 2025, within 30 days. The commission, headed by Anil Kumar Pundir, has also directed the developer to pay Rs 10,000 as compensation for mental agony and litigation costs.Gaur City residents Anita Kalia and her husband, Subedar Major Gajendar Kalia, had planned to build their dream home and decided to purchase a plot in Noida's Sector 124. The couple approached Bajwa Developers Ltd, which was operating in Noida in 2021, and paid Rs 25.2 lakh in instalments. However, the developer kept delaying the handover of the plot. When the couple visited the site of the plot allotted to them, they were shocked to find a house already constructed on it. They were subsequently told that the plot had been sold to someone else willing to pay a higher price.Aggrieved by the development, the couple approached the commission on April 9, 2025, seeking a refund of the entire amount of Rs 25.2 lakh, along with interest and compensation.Anita told the commission that she had booked a 150-square-yard plot in KT Block, Sunny Enclave, Sector 124, through an earnest money agreement with Bajwa Developers Ltd on September 21, 2021. The developer had allotted plot No. 526 T to her at the rate of Rs 16,800 per square yard.The couple paid Rs 25.2 lakh in instalments and subsequently sent a letter to the developer stating that no amount was outstanding and requesting the issuance of a possession letter. However, despite receiving the full payment, the developer failed to issue the possession letter. The complainant repeatedly tried to contact the company through phone calls and emails but received no resolution.Perturbed by the delay, the couple visited the plot and found a house constructed on it. The developer reportedly told them that they would not be given possession because the plot had been sold to someone else at a higher price. When the couple demanded a refund, the developer refused, compelling them to approach the consumer commission.The commission issued notices to the developer after admitting the complaint. However, the opposite party neither appeared before it nor submitted a written response. Consequently, on June 20, the commission ordered that the matter proceed ex parte."The plaintiff's ex-parte arguments were heard, and all available evidence on the file was examined. A perusal of the facts, circumstances, and records of the case clearly demonstrates that an agreement was reached between the plaintiff and the defendant, and all payments were made to the defendant in a timely manner. However, despite the payment, the defendant refused to hand over possession of the plot and instead handed over possession to someone else. The plaintiff has substantiated her claim by providing all evidence of the payment, payment slab, and agreement. The defendant's actions constitute a deficiency in service. articles.title: Iowa residents brace for a lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate bomb-making chemicals
articles.summary: Plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals, have residents in southeast Iowa worried that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems.
articles.body: DES MOINES, Iowa — Plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals that have become unusable and might explode if moved, have residents in southeast Iowa worried that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems. The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is set for Friday, and officials recommend that residents of a neighborhood in nearby Middletown begin vacating the area that morning. If they can’t leave their homes, they should stay inside and keep windows and doors closed. “The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals. The goal of this advisory is to provide the public with actionable information out of an abundance of caution to minimize lead exposure.” Officials also have released maps showing the potential for lead dust to drift north toward other communities. Some schools in the path of the plume have canceled classes. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but there are thousands more in the track of the plume. The vibrations from the two blasts will be quick but could break old windows in town. The resulting dust is expected to linger for no more than one hour, depending on wind speed, officials said. While the Army recommends washing cars and cleaning windowsills and outdoor surfaces, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough. Surrounding communities get late notice Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered. “The safety of our people and our neighbors is non‑negotiable,” Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse, commander of the plant, said at the time, acknowledging the volatility of the chemical compound used in munitions production. The Army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November. The Environmental Protection Agency on Nov. 13 approved an emergency permit, paving the way for Friday’s detonation. That permit required the Army to track the potential air and dust dispersion and notify the public five days in advance, prompting Sunday’s notification to communities as far as 100 miles (160 kilometers) away. Less than 20 miles (32 kilometers) northeast in Mediapolis, city officials were approached about allowing soil, water and air testing late last month. But they only learned of their potential exposure from the planned detonation Sunday, when the map put them dead-center in the dust exposure area. Mediapolis Community School District announced Tuesday that the “uncontrollable variables” prompted the decision to close school Friday, with no events or sports practices. The public library also is set to close, and the local fire department will hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles. The EPA will have a command center in Mediapolis to sample the air, soil and water during and after the detonation, according to city officials. But the city will do its own testing as well to try to assure concerned residents. “This is probably a first for me. I believe it’s a first for a lot of our citizens,” said Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker. “The biggest issue we’re having is the lack of information.” Even Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds’ office was first briefed Monday on the public advisory, her office said. News of the planned blasts also caught the attention of environmental and public health officials in Illinois. They urged the U.S. military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state following the detonations. Long-term storage leaves lead azide vulnerable The barrels of lead azide had been stored at the ammunition plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, public affairs specialist at the Army Sustainment Command. During a routine check earlier this year, they found that some of the water had evaporated, causing the lead azide to crystallize. That makes it more sensitive to friction and shock, thus “creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation,” according to an emergency permit approved last week by the EPA. Moving or relocating it posed an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation, officials said. Barati said that possibility increases in cold weather. “We’re really concerned about the weather situation,” Barati said on moving forward with Friday’s detonation. “We’re really concerned that it will detonate on its own.” The Army said it put together a panel of experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with the detonation plan. The barrels are surrounded above, below and on all sides with concrete, which is buried under soil. Sand barriers are stacked two stories high around the soil. During the detonation, the soil will be sprayed with water and the air will be misted to try to keep the majority of lead on Army property, Barati said. Young children are a particular concern for potential exposure Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa’s Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, said it is encouraging to see that the Army and the EPA are doing all they can to minimize the dust, but it’s still unknown how much will end up in the atmosphere and on surfaces. Lead is a neurological toxicant that can decrease brain activity and development, especially in young children, O’Shaughnessy said. He is particularly concerned for toddlers who are at the age of putting everything in their mouth. According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the contents of the drums using other chemicals were considered. But officials said any plan that involved handling the drums would increase the probability of accidental, fatal detonation.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s Nvidia debacle reveals America’s real problem: no skilled builders
articles.summary: New York Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says "five guys in tuxedos" shouldn't control the economy, but the real problem starts with manufacturing.
articles.body: If there’s anything more insufferable than New York Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's choreographed "on the go" interviews on social media... it’s AOC when she has a point. Her recent comment that we can’t have "five guys in tuxedos" control our national economy and security is, alas, reasonable in the wake of the Jensen Huang Nvidia debacle. But seizing and breaking up companies built by brilliant, entrepreneurial Americans (as she advocates) isn’t the answer (it’s also not constitutional, but that likely wouldn’t deter her). Socialism isn’t the solution here. It’s the problem. JENSEN HUANG OWES AMERICA AN APOLOGY, AND NVIDIA OWES INVESTORS ANSWERS And the leftist turn in our education system is why we’re stuck relying on foreign actors for America’s critical supply chains. Because even when we want to build here at home... we no longer have the ability. We all know the Nvidia facts by now. Jensen Huang, the company’s flamboyant, now former CEO, is accused of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. As part of that liaison, Huang may have sold billions of dollars' worth of America’s most advanced chips to the woman’s companies, potentially violating U.S. sanctions. A SPY TOOK OUT NVIDIA’S CEO. HERE’S HOW AMERICA STILL WINS THE AI RACE Huang ran NVIDIA like a potentate: 60 direct reports, no succession plan, and a reputation for abusing underlings. He also behaved like an adolescent in public. In short: maybe not the guy we want single-handedly embodying one of America’s biggest technological advantages. Adding to this vulnerability, NVIDIA doesn’t manufacture its chips; it designs them. Its highest-end chips are made by TSMC in Taiwan—80 miles off the coast of a nation that considers Taiwan its territory. AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD And TSMC operates two manufacturing plants inside mainland China. What could go wrong? The threat of China capturing Taiwan’s advanced facilities is so serious that TSMC and its Dutch equipment supplier, ASML, reportedly possess technology capable of remotely disabling critical manufacturing equipment. Consider that. The world’s most important chip manufacturer has a plan to disable its own factories to keep China from capturing them. And a European nation has the kill switch. KEY AMERICAN INDUSTRY SEEING BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM AS TRUMP'S RE-SHORING POLICIES PAY OFF Get the feeling we’re vulnerable here? So did both the Biden and Trump administrations. Bring It On Home Recognizing these vulnerabilities, in 2022 the Biden administration signed into law the CHIPS and Science Act to bring critical manufacturing home. TSMC received up to $6.6 billion in federal funding to build an advanced chip fabrication plant—a "fab"—in Arizona. Trump then prioritized manufacturing revival through tariffs and investment negotiations. In July 2026, TSMC raised its planned U.S. investment to $265 billion. There was only one problem. America—literally—couldn’t build the factory. CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE You read that right. The nation that built the Panama Canal and Hoover Dam, put men on the moon and invented the internet... lacked the expertise to build the plant. America must stop treating manufacturing—you know, actually building things—as a lesser occupation. To own the future—a safe future—we need electricians, pipefitters, welders, precision technicians and engineers. TSMC struggled to find workers experienced in specialized construction and equipment installation. So in 2023, it announced plans to bring approximately 500 specialized workers from Taiwan. American construction unions objected, of course, insisting qualified domestic workers were available. Eventually, a compromise emerged. But thousands of Taiwanese employees and their families still relocated to Arizona, creating an area known as Tiny Taipei. Taiwanese restaurants, businesses, and residential communities emerged around the project. One apartment complex became known as TSMC Village. And labor wasn’t the only problem. America’s regulatory morass further delayed construction, with TSMC spending $35 million to address 18,000 work rules. The Problem Continues TSMC’s first Arizona fab began producing chips in late 2024. A second is preparing for production, and a third is under construction. Yet worker shortages persist. In July 2026, TSMC CFO Wendell Huang (is everybody in chip tech named Huang?) acknowledged continuing shortages of construction workers. How can America lack the people for these jobs? Look at our education system. WINNING THE AI RACE MEANS BEATING CHINA ON INNOVATION, COST AND TRUST For decades, educators have emphasized four-year degrees while treating vocational training and skilled trades as an embarrassment. As podcaster Adam Carolla told this writer during a recent interview, "So now you attract a bunch of people… attracted to what is a socialist lifestyle. And now you put those people in charge of educating your kids. And how do you think that’s going to turn out?" Meanwhile, a semiconductor workforce study commissioned by the Semiconductor Industry Association projects tens of thousands of unfilled technical positions by 2030. Yet teachers’ unions continue pushing young Americans toward useless degrees and desk jobs increasingly threatened by AI—while the expertise needed to manufacture that technology grows overseas. All while the top foreign donors to American colleges remain shielded from scrutiny. It’s time for a reset. NVIDIA SPY CASE EXPOSES HOW FOREIGN AGENTS TARGET AMERICA’S CORPORATE ELITE: 'HE IS COMPROMISED' Then-Republican presidential candidate Sen. Marco Rubio understood this when he declared, at the fourth Republican presidential primary debate on November 10, 2015, "For the life of me, I don't know why we have stigmatized vocational education. Welders make more money than philosophers. We need more welders and less philosophers." Naturally, Rubio faced media backlash, with The Washington Post and The Associated Press rushing to fact-check welders’ and philosophers’ salaries (there’s a philosopher career track?). Rubio couldn’t have been more right. America must stop treating manufacturing—you know, actually building things—as a lesser occupation. That means technical high schools, apprenticeships, and community colleges committed to teaching useful skills. Above all, it requires a paradigm shift in how we think about education and teachers. To own the future—a safe future—we need electricians, pipefitters, welders, precision technicians and engineers. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION In short, people who know how to swing a damn hammer. Accurately. So enough with $100,000 in student loans for degrees in Hate America 101. If America wants manufacturing independence, it must rebuild the workforce—and the education system capable of training it. Otherwise, we’ll remain dependent on foreign labor to build the very factories intended to protect us from foreign dependence. articles.title: Iran’s oil leverage is weakening. That could push it toward escalation
articles.summary: Iran’s hold over the Strait of Hormuz is slipping, and experts warn that a cornered Tehran has tended to choose escalation over capitulation.
articles.body: Iran’s hold over the Strait of Hormuz is slipping, and experts warn that a cornered Tehran has tended to choose escalation over capitulation. Oil is flowing again despite continued Iranian attacks on shipping in the waterway, eroding the leverage Tehran has wielded against the United States since the war began. Now, Iran may be looking for ways to break the stalemate as US President Donald Trump piles economic pressure on the Islamic Republic in the hope of forcing it to make concessions. Iran rattled the global energy market at the outset of the conflict when it effectively shuttered the maritime chokepoint through which a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war. The price of oil surged globally, prompting some economists to warn of a worldwide recession should the closure continue. American consumers were dealt higher prices at the gas pump, and spiraling energy costs were seen as a major factor in big Republican losses in the US midterm election this month. Trump himself acknowledged that the war was partly to blame for his party’s defeat. But a global recession never materialized. Oil exports from the region are now close to pre-war levels, and the global market may soon have more crude than it needs. For Iran, that’s a problem. Iranian officials have nonetheless claimed victory, arguing that Tehran’s closure of the strait has already yielded major strategic gains. Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, made his country’s intention clear: “We want to impose a cost on the Americans that makes attacking Iran too expensive, and that serves as a deterrent.” A diminishing threat Experts say one of Iran’s main wartime strategies – exerting pressure on global energy markets – may now be losing its potency. Danny Citrinowicz, a senior fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies in Israel, said that Tehran has long sought to “internationalize” the cost of war. But “if oil prices continue to fall despite Iranian attacks, an important part of that strategy becomes less effective,” he told CNN. Oil prices have fallen sharply in recent weeks despite an escalation in Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The International Energy Agency attributes this to recovered Gulf exports, with oil supply expected to surpass demand in the fourth quarter for the first time since the outbreak of the Iran war in February. “It certainly seems that Iran is either unwilling or unable to prevent the flow of crude oil at present,” David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at the consultancy firm Capital Economics, told CNN, adding that “navigability in the strait is still far short of pre-crisis norms.” Ahria Roushanbakhti, head of the fuel desk at Axis Limited, the Middle East’s largest energy liquidity provider, said that while Iran may be losing some of its hold on the waterway, its ability to cause significant damage to energy infrastructure in the region remains worrying. An emboldened Iran Iran experts say that at this point in the conflict, Tehran is unlikely to dampen its demands but rather escalate its military operations to break the “neither war nor peace” stalemate with the US that is crippling Iran’s economy. Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said that Tehran appears more confident than ever after Trump’s midterm setback, celebrating the Republican Party’s losses. But oil prices dipped after the midterm results as fears eased that Trump would reignite the war and Tehran ramped up diplomacy with mediators. “Markets appear to be increasingly assuming that a return to full-scale war is unlikely and that oil supplies will gradually recover,” Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN. “But that assumption could change quickly if Iran decides to intensify the confrontation,” he said. That may be unfolding, as Iran already appears to be looking at other options to pressure the US back to the negotiating table. Added threats by the US may even force Iran into more proactive measures that would be costly for both sides, experts said. Tehran’s options The conflict has escalated rapidly in recent days after a period of relative calm. The region saw a series of back-and-forth attacks by Iran and allied Houthi rebels in Yemen on Gulf countries, as well as US attacks on Iranian territory around the strait. Presented with the possibility of perceived capitulation or military escalation, Iran’s hardline regime has tended to choose the latter despite the cost, experts say. “When it feels cornered, it may become more aggressive, not less,” Citrinowicz said. Iran may choose to increase pressure on tankers using the US-supported route in the Strait of Hormuz, said Azizi, of the International Crisis Group. It may also choose to disrupt ship-to-ship transfers of oil, or target Gulf infrastructure or alternative export routes that allow Gulf countries to bypass some Tehran’s restrictions in Hormuz, he said. Tehran also appears to be lowering the threshold for retaliation. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Tuesday said it targeted American radars in Bahrain following unspecified “US drone violations of Iran’s airspace.” It has also warned Bahrain’s Sunni rulers against mistreatment of the majority Shiite population. Iran has warned countries against allowing the US to use their territory to attack it. National security chief Rezaei said last week that “all military bases… from Western Asia to Europe, will be legitimate targets.” “There will be no safe distance or safe haven for aggressors,” he warned, adding that “no base will remain immune.” This shows that Iran may not only be looking to expand its scope of operations, but is now “signaling that even violations of its airspace could trigger attacks against American assets,” Azizi said. Others believe there is not much else the Islamic Republic can do that can bring Washington to agree to a deal that works for Iran. Parsi of the Quincy Institute said that further action by Iran will not make a difference. What could make a change, he said, is the one thing that Iranians are disinclined to do: give Trump a “symbolic” victory that is “ego-soothing and face-saving.” The Iranians, he said, are more opposed to a symbolic loss than a substantive one, which only adds to the stalemate. Meanwhile, a third US aircraft carrier strike group recently entered US Central Command’s area of responsibility, where it is expected to – at least temporarily – join ongoing operations that include enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports and escorting commercial ships willing to transit the strait. Washington may be misjudging Iran’s breaking point, experts said. Tehran’s latest operations fit into a “broader shift in Iranian military thinking toward more proactive deterrence,” Azizi said. “If the leadership concludes that its leverage over Hormuz is weakening while the American blockade continues to impose economic costs, it may decide to go further, potentially even challenging US naval forces more directly,” he said. This would be considerably riskier, he said “but Iran may see it as necessary to break the blockade rather than allow its position to deteriorate gradually.”

articles.title: TOI Bharat Abroad: From visa uncertainty to a victory for Indian students
articles.summary: Hello and welcome to TOI Bharat Abroad.
articles.body: Hello and welcome to TOI Bharat Abroad.The American student visa maze has thrown up a rare bit of good news: Two court rulings have put separate Trump administration curbs on hold. In Britain, a young Indian-origin designer is turning alarms into lights and vibrations for people who cannot hear them. And in Pennsylvania, a family from Bihar has brought Chhath home by building a makeshift ghat in its own backyard.THE BIG STORYUS student visas get a reprieveFor international students in the US, the past few months have been a lesson in reading the fine print. Now, two court decisions have offered some breathing space. In separate cases, federal judges have blocked measures introduced by the Trump administration that threatened to make it harder for foreign students to stay in the country and gain practical work experience during their courses.The relief is particularly significant for Indian students. At nearly 3.4 lakh, they form the largest group of international students in the US, making changes to student visa rules a major concern for families, universities and employers on both sides.The big pictureThe first ruling came on November 16, when US District Judge F Dennis Saylor IV set aside the Department of Homeland Security's final rule that sought to end the long-standing 'duration of status' system for international students on F-1 visas, exchange visitors on J-1 visas and representatives of foreign media.Under the existing arrangement, students can remain in the US for the duration of their academic programme, provided they maintain their immigration status and meet the relevant requirements. The administration's proposed replacement would have capped their stay at four years, requiring those who needed more time to apply for extensions.The rule could also have restricted students' ability to change their course, major or education level, transfer institutions or pursue further studies. The court has now set aside the regulation in its entirety, preserving the existing framework. An appeal by the administration, however, remains possible.Why it mattersA second ruling, issued on November 17, offered relief on another front. US District Judge Julia Kobick granted a preliminary injunction against two directives that had narrowed eligibility for Curricular Practical Training (CPT), which allows F-1 students to take up internships and practical training linked to their academic courses.For more than 35 years, students could generally qualify for CPT when the training was directly related to their field of study and formed an integral part of the curriculum. The new interpretation suggested that an internship would qualify only if it was compulsory for every student enrolled in that degree programme. That could have put elective, credit-bearing internships at risk.The judge's order prevents the government from enforcing the revised interpretation while the legal challenge continues. It does not, however, guarantee approval for every student. Universities must still assess applications individually, and students need formal CPT authorisation before starting work.Taken together, the decisions offer some relief to international students at a time when uncertainty around US visas has become a growing concern. For Indian students weighing up the cost of an American degree against the prospect of building a career there, the court rulings are a welcome pause in an increasingly complicated journey.Read full storyTurning alarms into lightA fire alarm goes off in a hotel room. The sound is loud, urgent and impossible to miss. Unless, of course, you cannot hear it. That everyday problem inspired 23-year-old Indian-origin designer Gargi Agrawalla to build a device that could make such warnings accessible to deaf and hard-of-hearing people.Born profoundly deaf, Agrawalla developed SIVO.GO as her final-year project at Loughborough University in the UK. The idea came from her own experiences staying in hotels, where emergency alarms, doorbells and other room signals were not always visible or tactile.The device uses artificial intelligence to recognise fire alarms and doorbells without relying on Wi-Fi or cloud processing. It can also detect knocks and door movement. Instead of depending on sound, it alerts users through colour-coded lights, symbols on a screen and vibrations.For Agrawalla, the problem is particularly personal. She uses a cochlear implant, but when hearing devices are removed during sleep or while showering, important alerts can easily be missed. SIVO.GO is designed to bridge those gaps and help users feel safer and more independent.The project won the UK James Dyson Award earlier this year, earning Agrawalla £5,000 to develop the prototype further. Her next steps include refining the technology and testing it with users. She had previously designed jewellery that could be worn with hearing devices, with the pieces going into production last year.Read full storyOFFBEATHow Chhath travelled from Buxar to PennsylvaniaChhath Puja is usually pictured along the riverbanks of Bihar, with devotees standing in the water to offer prayers to the setting and rising Sun. But in Pennsylvania, a family from Buxar has found a way to recreate that familiar setting thousands of miles from home. The secret? A pond in their own backyard.Tarkeshwar Tiwari and his wife Bharti, who hail from Sonbarsa village in Bihar's Buxar district, joined hands with members of the local Indian community to organise the four-day festival in the US. To recreate the atmosphere of a traditional Chhath ghat, they set up an artificial pond at their residence and decorated the premises for the rituals. Traditional Chhath songs helped bring a little of Bihar to Pennsylvania.For Bharti, who has observed the fast for 18 years, the celebrations are also about ensuring that younger generations remain connected to their roots. The family hopes the festival will introduce more people in the diaspora to Bihar's folk traditions.And Pennsylvania is not alone. From New Jersey to London, Indian families marked Chhath near lakes, canals and other local water bodies. The rituals remain the same, but devotees have to follow local sunrise and sunset timings when offering arghya. After all, the Sun does not run on Indian Standard Time.Read full storyDID YOU KNOWNRI SPOTLIGHTLEMONCHILLINews that hits like a meme, but sticks like a fact. articles.body: CHENNAI: Kolathur MLA V S Babu died following a cardiac arrest at MGM Healthcare on Thursday, more than 70 days after he was admitted with a respiratory illness.Babu had been under intensive care since his admission on September 9. “Despite comprehensive medical management and the best efforts of our multidisciplinary clinical team, his condition continued to deteriorate. articles.title: U.S. judge says ICE ‘made a mockery of court orders’ in Colorado
articles.summary: A federal judge said the ICE agency “made a mockery of court orders” in ​Colorado after instantly ‌re-arresting a man whom the judge had ordered released.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A federal judge said on Wednesday the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency “made a mockery of court orders” in ​Colorado and that the court found government officials in contempt for instantly ‌re-arresting a man whom the judge had ordered released. U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney declined to take any further action because she said the officials had “cured the contempt ​by ceasing the practice at issue” as sworn by an official ​in court. “ICE’s new ‘policy’ of immediately re-detaining petitioners following release made ⁠a mockery of court orders mandating petitioners’ immediate release,” the judge ​wrote, according to court records in the U.S. District Court for the District ​of Colorado. At least 18 people in Colorado have been held in detention longer than they should have been or have been re-arrested within minutes of their judge-ordered release ​in the past six weeks, CPR News, the news division of ​Colorado Public Radio, reported. The report said that immigration attorneys estimated the number may be higher ‌given ⁠that some immigrants represented themselves. ICE, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security, has been the face of Republican President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and deportation drive that rights groups say has violated free speech and due ​process rights. Human rights ​groups also say ⁠the crackdown has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling. The Trump ​administration has maintained that its actions aim to improve ​domestic security ⁠and are in compliance with the law. ICE and DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on what the judge said on ⁠Wednesday. Democrats, who ​won majorities in both chambers of Congress ​in the midterm elections earlier this month, say they aim to hold the Trump administration accountable ​for its immigration policies.
